utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Turning to the Registrar, would you have the accused brought in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are the interpreters prepared? Does the Prosecutor hear? Good morning. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You do. Mr. Hayman, Mr. Nobilo, good morning. Do you hear me? General Blaskic, do you hear me? GENERAL BLASKIC: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Everything is working properly. We can now resume our work. I would like to tell the Prosecutor that the Tribunal has decided that it would sit this afternoon and if the expert witness has not completed his testimony this morning, he will continue this afternoon, starting at 3 o'clock. Therefore we are resuming our hearing and I give the floor to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and your Honours. Before we start with the testimony of Mr. Donia, I would request that in respect of eight items that were marked for identification yesterday, starting with the organogram that I referred to in my opening statement as the first item, the second item being my letter to Messrs Hayman and Nobilo in respect of witnesses; the third item was the notes, the outline that was referred to and the French translation; the fifth items -- items 5 through 8 were various maps referred to by Mr. Donia, I would request, your Honour, that all those items be admitted into evidence and I would request, your Honour, that in respect of the second item, which is my letter to Messrs Hayman and Nobilo, that that be maintained under seal pending a decision by this court on a motion that is pending before it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We certainly have no objection to maintaining the letter concerning the identity of witnesses under seal. I would say with respect to the other matters, first of all the diagram of the purported structure of the HVO, that was used in argument by counsel. There has been no testimony that it's accurate. There has been no testimony as to its source. It's premature to admit that diagram into evidence. With respect to Mr. Donia's notes and his chronology, I was reviewing the chronology last night. This is the item that has already been provided to the court, to which we do not object. I have no idea who wrote this chronology. This chronology spans from the 6th century to 1995, well after the end of the charges in this case. For example, there's an entry of 9th July 1993 regarding a meeting between a Mr. Owen, Croatian President Tudjman and others. Was this witness there? Was he present at the meeting? Has he reviewed documents? I have no idea. We have no idea of the foundation of the information for this outline, and I'm surprised that the Prosecutor would move for its admission at this time. It may well be proper to admit it later but it is certainly premature. The same goes, I submit, for the outline of his testimony. We have not even heard his direct testimony concerning the contents of this outline, much less any cross-examination. The maps -- we have not been told yet where the maps came from, at least with respect to all of them. There has been a general reference to a census and so forth. I do not expect there to be an issue with the maps, but I think we need to have the sources clarified before they are admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First, I would like to shed some light on the problem of terminology. I am given the French word "piece d'identification". I know the expression in French "piece a conviction" for evidence. I do not know whether the interpretation was meant to talk about "piece a conviction", that is evidence, Prosecutor evidence. Did you mean Prosecutor evidence or inculpatory evidence? We talk about this terminology and maps. Did you mean these to be inculpatory evidence? Is that what you meant by that? Do you want us to put the list of witnesses under seal? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do not mean they are inculpatory evidence, your Honour. I just ask the court to admit them for its review and I would ask that they be admitted for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now we are talking about a problem of terminology here. I do not really -- I'm not that familiar with your system, so when you talk about evidence, I wasn't sure what you meant. I thought you meant it to be Prosecutor evidence. That's why I asked the interpreters if that's the -- what is the correct term? Are we talking about prosecutorial evidence? Are you saying that we have to file identifying documents? I do not really know quite know what that means, this "piece d'identification" in French. Do you want filed documents as documents which the Tribunal will be able to use in its deliberations before it arrives at its judgement? All right. So we are talking about Prosecutor's evidence. So we have now solved the problem of terminology. Mr. Hayman, do you agree with the terminology expressed that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand the concept. I am not sure I know what French phrase will be used for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: At least if we understand what we mean by concept we are all right. The second point, that is as far as keeping these under seal, I have no problem with that. As far as the other documents are concerned, Mr. Hayman is contesting them personally. I will, of course, consult with my colleagues, but I would lean rather towards favouring what is being discussed here be put in as prosecutorial evidence for the Tribunal, which can then be contested later by the Defence, if it wants, during its cross-examination, during which, Mr. Hayman, you could bring another map or you could contest the chronological outline that the expert witness gave evidence. I myself could not tell you whether really it was in 1342 that the Franciscan mission was set up in Bosnia. Perhaps it was in 1343 or 1341. All that could be contested as everything could be contested. Personally I will consult my colleagues but I think this should be filed and then afterwards the Defence can contest things. If you wish to show another map with another set of arguments, all right. For the time being the only thing I need to do is whether we should admit these today or whether we should admit these after your cross-examination. For that I will discuss it with my colleagues. (Pause.) Mr. Hayman, Mr. Harmon, the Tribunal has decided that it will admit all the documents right now, all of the Prosecutor's evidence. Of course when you do your cross-examination or in the following weeks, at any point in the proceedings throughout the trial you, Mr. Hayman, of course can and will be permitted by the Tribunal -- will supply any other documents or you can contest the organisational chart or the map, do anything you like. The comment I am making to the Defence today -- I would like to say this so things be clear in the future -- goes in the opposite direction. That is when you have documents to produce, Mr. Hayman, in theory they will be presented to the Tribunal. They will be attached as evidence and the Prosecutor also will be able to contest them at the point that he wishes to. We have now completed with this incident and I give you back the floor: Mr. Hayman, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know to whom the floor was being returned, your Honour. Thank you. I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I had given the floor back to the Prosecutor, but unless you have something you would like to add, but I think that the incident is now closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I accept -- I am not contesting the court's point or the court's ruling, but so we have clarity of terms and concepts, it is foreign to me that a document would be admitted for its truth, for the truth of the matters asserted when there has been no testimony of the source or accuracy or authenticity of the document. For example, assertions that in 1992 and 1993, which are central to the time period of this case, that certain things happened. For example, on page 4 of the chronology. If those are now accepted as proven facts, because this chronology has been admitted, that troubles me a great deal. I simply want to state that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think what separates us is a conceptual problem and a legal culture. We cannot throughout this trial keep opposing one legal system against the other. As I said to you yesterday, the Tribunal guarantees an equitable, just trial for the accused, and also allows the accused -- sorry -- the Prosecution to prove what it has charged. The problem is a very simple one, I think, and I do not want us to be become overly complicated. So for the last time I would like to speak to that question, because the Tribunal will not come back to this issue. You have every right -- I turn now to General Blaskic -- you can contest the entire document. You can contest, for example, Mr. Hayman, the chronology that was presented. I think, as far as the history of the Balkans, we could bring in ten different experts and perhaps they would have ten different interpretations. You can go from the 6th to the 7th century, start from that point. You can go back to 1992, 1993. You will have every possible right in order to contest anything you like. We did not say and the Tribunal is not stating today that this is being considered as historical truth. We all know in this Tribunal that historical truths essentially are evanescent. As it stands now, this is simply a document that the witness submitted, which you accepted to hear, whom you accepted to hear. He has the right to say what he wants. This is a witness who is brought in by the Prosecutor. He has the right to say since you said this that in 1992 or 1993 -- I do not really know what fact you were pointing to -- that there was a meeting. You will contest that. You will contest the military organisational chart. You have every right to contest everything that you want to contest but for the time being we are hearing a prosecution witness. You will have every right to cross-examine or every right to say or to ask him whether his sources are based on what or, in fact, where his sources come from. So I believe, Mr. Hayman, that for the next six months of trial we should not constantly bring about a clash of different legal systems. What we are trying to do is to have a just and equitable trial. I will insist on this warmly. It was never said in the Rules of the Tribunal in Rule 1 that we will apply the procedures that Mr. Hayman is used to using in Common Law in Los Angeles. We never said that, Mr. Hayman. We are simply applying in this Tribunal a procedure that is just and equitable and I claim when one attaches this to the case file of the Tribunal the Tribunal will use it, but it also means you have every right to contest the document at the time when you will consider it opportune to do so, whether it be Monday, today or with your historical experts and the tribunal will accept your experts if you wish to call them. I will give you back the floor, but I would not like that every time there is a document presented we go back to the same question of sources. They can be contested when you like. This is what I wanted to say to you. I give you the floor for the last time on this point. Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We are not seeking to aggravate the court and I want to assure the court of that. I am trying to make clear for our own purposes so the proceedings will move smoothly what the requirements are for the admission of exhibits and we need not address that at further length now. I am not seeking to delay the proceedings. Believe me, we want the proceedings to move forward quickly. I think it is important at some point that the requirements for the admission of substantive evidence be clear to the parties because we do come, some of us from different legal cultures. It is important that I understand the court's requirements so I can abide by them, because we do want to abide by them, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. With this final word on which there is consensus, we can close this discussion. If I have to speak firmly, it is because the incident and discovery of documents will be treated as they have just been treated. I claim along with my colleagues that we will perfectly respect the inter-party aspects of the proceedings. It is now 10.22. I give you back the floor, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and your Honours. The Prosecutor would call Mr. Donia back to the stand. If the usher can step out ... thank you. As Mr. Donia is coming in, Mr. President, could the usher just give exhibits 5, 7 and 8 back to Mr. Donia? . Exhibit 6, per the Registrar's records, is the map on the wall. I ask that, your Honour, just to facilitate the proceedings so that Mr. Donia can move back and forth between these documents. (Witness enters court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I give you the floor to answer the questions that the Prosecutor will ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe we left off yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Naturally I would like to remind Mr. Donia that you are under oath and you have been since yesterday. You do not have to take the oath again but of course the oath you took yesterday covers your entire testimony so long as you will be in front of the Trial Chamber. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Donia, I believe we left off yesterday with the exhibit before you, exhibit 5, and with the request to the usher if we could put that back on the ELMO. I stand corrected. It's exhibit 8. If we could take that out of the sleeve, Mr. Usher. There is a bit of a glare on that. Thank you. I believe, Mr. Donia, if you turn back to Prosecutor's Exhibit 8, that's the exhibit that we left off on yesterday, where you were explaining essentially the full extent of the Bosnian State during the time period in the late 14th century; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 12th-14th centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we move to that, can you just again with your pointer point to the outline of the full extent of that territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian State began in the late 12th century in this small, almost circular area and subsequently expanded to include almost all of what is present day Bosnia and came to include much of the Dalmatian coast and also that part of the Dalmatian coast which had previously been ruled by the Nemanja dynasty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say, Mr. Donia, that by the late 14th century, looking at the full extent of the Bosnian Empire, it encompassed large portions of present day Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Significant portions of it. It was not an empire; it was a kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. A kingdom. Thank you. I believe we were next going to move to the kingdom of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we begin with that, if I may request the usher to hand an exhibit out. I believe the number sequentially at this point, your Honour, is Prosecutor's Exhibit 9. Mr. Donia, I put the map on the ELMO. You have freedom to refer to it as you so wish, but could you tell us a little bit about the historical kingdom of Croatia going back to the Middle Ages, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The kingdom of Croatia originally emerged from a group of South Slavic tribal leaders who were vassals of the Francs. After the death of Charlemagne in 814 they increasingly came to assert their independence. Vladislav who ruled starting in 821 was the first of these leaders to style himself as a Duke of the Croatians and Dalmatians. By legend and documentation the zenith of the Croatian holdings was reached under King Tomislav, whose dates are uncertain, but he ruled roughly in the period from the very early 10th century, say around 910 until about 920 or 925. He was crowned King of Croatia with the permission of the Pope and has since become a very important figure in the iconography of Croatian national history. In fact on the map which is a map of Croatia at the time of Tomislav, one sees a picture of the statue of Tomislav that greets the visitor today to Zagreb on walking out of the main railroad station, a very stately and monumental statue right in front of the central railroad station in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are pointing to the upper right-hand corner of the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Subsequent rulers lost and then regained much of the authority that Tomislav had. The foundation or strongest point and capital of this Croatian kingdom was in the area of the central and northern Dalmatian coast, about where this arrow begins. It was extended on the basis of conquests and subsequently Bans or governors were appointed for various areas, Pannonia, Dalmatia and Bosnia. The Croatian kingdom reached difficult times in the very late 11th century as the last holder of the Crown died out and for a period of about ten years there were conflicts over who would hold the thrown. This came to an end in the year 1102, which is an important date in Croatian history, with the Pacta Conventa, which is referenced in my chronology, in which a group of Croatian nobles met with the Hungarian King and agreed to become united with the Hungarian Crown. Croatian historians portray this as a voluntary submission. Hungarian historians tend to portray it more as a result of a conquest, but it had great significance in that until 1918, all the way from 1102 until 1918, Croatia was a part of the Crown of Hungary and the Crown of Hungary carried the title the kingdom of Hungary and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 1918 is the end of the first world war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. So for, what, eight centuries or more this was the case. This is very important, because it meant that throughout this period Croatian nobles had a diet which they attended with greater or lesser regularity, and was attached to the Hungarian Crown. 1102, however, is the date at which the Medieval Croatian empire -- kingdom, excuse me, lost its independence and was for one purpose to a greater or lesser extent subjected to Hungarian domination or influence right up through the next many centuries. The Croatian kingdom was to become in the 20th century the basis of claims for territorial accusation by Croatian nationalists. Some of those were reasonably based and others of them get rather outlandish, but certainly one can see that on the map the territory that the Medieval kingdom encompassed -- Medieval kingdom of Croatia encompassed included virtually all, nearly all Bosnia. I would like to turn briefly, after having discussed that, to the Serbian empire, which at times also exerted an influence in the land that became Bosnia -- was Bosnia in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we move to the Serbia map, would it be fair to say, Mr. Donia, that, looking at the last two exhibits, there are vast reaches of land that overlap one another for the high watermark of the Republic of Croatia under Tomislavgrad in the late 19th century and the high watermark for the Kingdom of Bosnia in the 14th century?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the characteristic of these Medieval empires. One never knows how extensive the control of the Croatian Kings was over this northern area, for example, of so-called Pannonian Croatia. The attention of later chroniclers was particularly drawn by important events like battles and coronations, and these are two of the battles that took place, but as far as the degree of day-to-day control exercised and also questions of identity of the people in these kingdoms, much is not known.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we move to the Serbian map, we would like to introduce Exhibit 9, the historical map of the kingdom of Croatia, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have no objection if we could learn who created the map, whether this witness did or did it come from some other text or treaties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is a relevant question. Mr. Donia, did you draw this map? I want to tell you, Mr. Donia, that the Defence objection allows me to make this clarification. Before you came in this morning there was an incident involving contesting possibly of all of these documents. They have been tendered into the file. Let me tell you that the Tribunal has decided that all the documents, including these today or those that will be coming tomorrow from either of the parties, will be tendered to the case file. For the time being they are documents in the case file which will help the judges to deliberate. They can, therefore, be totally contested, as they were today by the Defence. Therefore the Defence question is relevant. We're asking you what sources you are using so the day that there is cross-examination you may be able to answer properly. This is a question I would like you to answer. Did you draw up this map or did you find it in documents and if you did find them in documents, could you cite them, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The map came from a book entitled "The Serbs: History, Myth and the Destruction of Yugoslavia", published by Yale University Press this year, 1997. This is the Serbian map, 1196-1355. The prior map, Mr. President, the one that's currently on the ELMO, is from a book entitled -- it's by Stjepan Antoljak -- "Pregled hrvatske povijesti", published in Split, Croatia in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Generally speaking, Mr. Donia, therefore, if you do not mind, I would like you to draw us up a list for this afternoon or tomorrow that you would give to the Tribunal through the Registry, a list in which you would summarise the text from which these maps came and, of course, it will be given to the Defence and will be put into the record of the Tribunal. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll do that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next map that we will address ourselves to is the map of Medieval Serbia. If I can hand it to the usher. For the purposes of the record, this is exhibit 10. Now, Mr. Donia, before we actually turn to the map, you had some preliminary comments that you wanted to give to the court concerning the Medieval Serbian area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In contrast to the Croatian kingdom, the Serbian kingdom emerged further to the south and east and ended up very much within the cultural and religious influence of Constantinople and therefore Eastern Orthodoxy. This is not how it began because in the year 1077 the land actually was ruled by a ruler Constantine Bodin, who ruled as a Catholic. But under the rule of Stefan Nemanja, which began in 1168, one sees this transition or emphasis on association with orthodoxy. That was confirmed later in this period of the Serbian empire when Stefan II, who was the son and successor of Nemanja, was crowned first by a papal legate in 1217 and then by a representative of the Eastern empire in 1222. The Serbian empire underwent a development somewhat like that of the Bosnian and Croatian in that it began in a smaller area adjacent to the Adriatic Sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you turning to the map and pointing to that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am pointing to the darkened area on this map, which was the core original Serbian empire. You see the names Zeta, Raska and Hum, which were areas or regions that were united under Stefan Nemanja. This darkened area is indicated here at the time of his abdication in 1196 came to be the area that was then a part of Serbia. It subsequently expanded both to the north and to the east and to the south and came to encompass substantial territory, which again became important in the 20th century as the basis for claims for the expanding Serbian state. Religion was important to the rulers of all these Medieval states on the basis of their alliances with the east and west. Perhaps more important than any cultural or personal piety attributes to many of these leaders in any case was their position in the alliances of the time between the Hungarian Kingdom to the north, the Byzantine Empire to the east and various political forces to the west and up into Bosnia. The period of multi-national empires really came to an end because of pressure from the emerging challenge of the Ottoman Empire, which is represented on this map in what is present day Asiatic Turkey. Also on this map are represented the two very important conflicts with the Ottoman Empire, the battle of Naritza, 1371 and the battle at Kosovo Polje in 1389. Both of these battles were styled as losses to the Serbian kingdom. The battle of Kosovo Polje in 1389 assumed great significance in the late 1980s as it became the basis for asserting nationalist claims by Serbian President Milosevic. The nature of that battle, however, is very much debated by historians in terms of who won and who emerged victorious. It is unquestionably true that the Serbian empire in somewhat reduced form continued for some decades after that battle. Nevertheless, the tide of Ottoman conquests in south-eastern Europe was well advanced by the year 1389.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Going back to the map, Exhibit 10, can you point to the essentially high watermark or the furthest reaches of the kingdom of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The far reaches include really all of south-eastern Europe but down almost to the Aegean Sea in most places, up into what is present day Serbia -- the Drina river is here; that is the boundary with Bosnia -- into the south sort of Central Bosnia and Hum, which was the term used at the time for what is present day Herzegovina. So this extends over what is today Greece and what is Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Once again would it be fair to say that these Medieval states, be it Croatia at its high watermark, Bosnia at its high watermark, or Serbia at its high watermark overlapped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and, in fact, there is probably not a square centimetre of land in the entire region that couldn't be claimed by at least 2 or 3 empires at the time if one wished to also include Hungary and Venice and the Byzantine Empire and the Ottomans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Obviously the Ottoman Empire and the taking over of the Balkans by the Ottoman Empire dramatically changed the composition of the Balkans, but what conclusions do you, as a historian, make about the events or the State of Medieval or the Medieval Balkan States just prior to the Ottoman Empire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Medieval Balkan States had all seen their high water marks by the time that the Ottomans entered Europe. Some were gone already. In fact, Croatia was by that time a part of the Hungarian Crown. Others were weakened by the existing battles by the Ottomans. The nature of those states, I think, is very important to understand. They were really emerging tribal leaders striving for greater status and power. Their degree of control is always subject to question. It principally was a matter of their using armed retinues and vassals, which themselves often held better control of the land, and allying themselves based on religious affiliation with and against neighbouring rivals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, is what happened in the Balkan States from the 10th century on to the 4th (sic) century consistent with what was happening throughout Europe throughout this time-frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally I think it was, yes. There are some differences. Perhaps the process of state formation was more advanced in other places than here, but the similar pattern of the emergence of a feudal society superseding a tribal one is indeed very similar. Later on there are further similarities that would suggest particularly parallels with areas of Eastern Europe in the Polish and Russian areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, before we proceed on, turning back to the ELMO and Exhibit 10, the kingdom of Serbia, what is the source for that map, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the book I just cited, "the Serbs: history, myth and the destruction of Yugoslavia" published by Yale University Press this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecutor would offer Exhibit 10 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President? We now come to an area or a period of time post the battle of Kosovo Polje in 1389 and the rise of the Ottoman Empire, do we not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit about the Ottoman Empire and its impact historically and moving in chronological order its impact on the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Ottoman Empire was in some respects a different kind of empire than the Medieval Bosnian kingdoms. It originated in the Turkic tribes of Anatolia, that is in Asia, across the Bosphorus and was highly organised as an empire of conquest. It is forays into south-eastern Europe resulted in successive triumphs and slowly it was able to conquer much of south-eastern Europe, in fact laying siege on two occasions to the city of Vienna, the latest in 1687. The conquest of the Ottoman Empire in Bosnia and in areas immediately adjacent to Bosnia changed the social landscape in very important ways. First of all, the Ottoman Empire was Islamic and brought with it a religious faith which prior to that time had only fragmentary presence in the Balkans. While there are very few instances of forced conversions by the Ottoman Empire in Bosnia and in the Balkans more generally, there were many conversions to Islam in Bosnia itself. The significance of these conversions can't be emphasised too much, because in other areas of the Balkans one did not see this kind of conversion to Islam. So a historical explanation is called for, which is a matter of great controversy. As I indicated, the present Bosnian Muslim historians tend to look to the Medieval Bosnian Church, which they frequently believe to be Bogomil as the source of the people who converted to Islam. They pointed out that many of these converts were members of the nobility or land-owning class and had to gain their retention of lands and privileges under the Ottoman Empire. What we find is that these conversions, and there were conversions in all directions in the first 150 years of Ottoman Rule, substantially changed the demographic character or the religious character of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you say there were conversions in all directions, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were conversions from Catholicism to Orthodoxy, from Orthodoxy to Catholicism and from both of those faiths to Islam. One finds a fluidity, if you will, of religious change. People felt relatively free to adopt different religions without serious adverse consequences. What that suggests to me is that the communities of religion were at that time not yet formed with firm boundaries. People thought of themselves as belonging to a particular local community and the search for a religious affiliation was an important one, but one which could be pursued without adverse consequences in many instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you can give us a time-frame, Mr. Donia. Starting from the battle of Kosovo Polje in 1389, what time-frame do you give for these religious conversions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1463 is the date that is normally accepted for the subjugation of Bosnia by the Ottomans. In the 140 years from 1463 -- perhaps the early decades of the 17th century are the times that we see these conversions taking place, and in general the latter half of the 15th and the rest of the 16th centuries are times of great religious and demographic change in Bosnia. I think I am ready for the next map, if you would like to...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could have with the court's permission the next map handed to the witness, which I believe is Exhibit 11. (Next map handed). If we can turn to the map Exhibit 11, Mr. Donia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment. The source of this map, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President and your Honours. I do not have the precise citation here. It is an Atlas of Croatian History, which I can provide you perhaps after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can take a break -- at the mid-morning break, your Honour, we will bring the book down with the source and provide it to your Honours. Why don't you proceed, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This map shows the Ottoman Empire's boundaries with its neighbours to the north-west and here in the Dalmatian area in the south-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are pointing to the map on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. It suggests, first of all, that the Bosnia we now come to know on contemporary maps existed largely in the Ottoman Empire as an area of Ottoman administration. This triangle that becomes so familiar. I mentioned that the demographic structure of Bosnia was changed substantially by conversions. The second major way in which it was changed during Ottoman years was through migration. Critical to that process was the establishment of the so-called military frontier. I will just run the area where that frontier was established. The origins of the military frontier go back to the desire of both the Habsburg Empire and the Ottoman Empire to fortify the boundary between them with a warrior class which was prepared either to defend the territory or participate in further assaults or protection of the boundary lands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is that called in Bosnian Serbo-Croatian? What is that known as, that military frontier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's called the Krijina. The result was that the Habsburg Empire, which ruled this area on the other side of the boundary, established boundary zones which they encouraged migration into and in particular bestowed freedom of religion and property on those people who chose to move there, principally of the Orthodox persuasion. So in the centuries of Ottoman Rule from about 1600 on, one sees the development of this so call military frontier area, which on this map is represented in a lighter shade of pink all round the boundaries of the Ottoman Empire in what was then Habsburg territory and clearly part of what historically were Croatian lands. So the result of that was the migration of thousands of Serbian Orthodox people to the area of a boundary between the Ottomans and the Habsburgs. On the Turkish side or Ottoman side, if you will, of that boundary a similar process occurred. Those frontier areas were fortified in some cases by Muslims and in many cases by Orthodox, who were also drawn to that region. Migration further continued as the Ottoman Empire later on in that area began to recede and some of these areas were abandoned by other settlers and Orthodox in particular came to move into those areas. The long and short of that is that the earlier years of Ottoman administration were very good ones for the Serbian Orthodox population from a demographic standpoint. They were less advantageous to Catholics. Part of the reason for that was that the Ottomans established a so-called millet system in which they provided limited autonomy or organisation to peoples of the book, that is those who were viewed as sharing the book with Muslims. There was an Orthodox millet system and a Jewish millet system which were very important for this area. The third development -- I have mentioned two developments that have changed the demographic character of the area. One was the conversions, two was migration and the third characteristic was economic and social development. The period of the 16th century was one of considerable prosperity in the Ottoman Empire and led to the growth of cities throughout Bosnia and, in fact, throughout the western part of the empire. Those cities became overwhelmingly Muslim in composition. There were others living in them. Jewish populations, for example, in various cities from 1492 at the time of the Sephardic emigration from Spain into Croatia were an important part of those cities. However, it is from this time that the Muslim demographic occupation of those cities truly dates. Later in the years of Ottoman administration the noble class or military class of Muslims gradually acquired greater authority over the peasants of Bosnia, and while there were some Christian peasants, Orthodox and Catholic who remained free, many entered into a status in which they owed obligations to Muslim landlords. This was a development that was very common in one form or another throughout Eastern Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries. It led to the rise of social tensions between the Christian and Muslim population, the Christian population meaning both the Serbian Orthodox population and the Catholic population. That came to a situation in the 19th century where some of those conflicts developed into peasant rebellions. But in the early years of the Ottoman administration, that first 150 to 200 years it was a time of relative urbanisation, growth and important changes in religious affiliation and migration that truly shook up the demographic character of Bosnia from its Medieval times. The period of Ottoman administration lasted until 1878. In 1878 an important changing of the guard occurred. I think we are perhaps ready to look at the next map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, with the court's permission, we can turn to Exhibit 12. Mr. President and your Honours, I did not forget with the last map to introduce it into evidence but at the break I will get the source of that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed? Mr. Donia, turning to Exhibit 12?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have the source for this, Mr. President, if you wish. It's the historical Atlas of East Central Europe prepared by Paul Robert Magocsi and published by University of Toronto Press in 1993. This map shows the Ottoman Empire at the time just prior to this changing of the guard in 1878. It shows the Kingdom of Croatia and Slovenia which was at that time, as we mentioned earlier, a part of the Crown of Hungary and the Kingdom of Dalmatia surrounding this Ottoman area of Bosnia. It also shows that in this area around the city of Belgrade an autonomous area has arisen known as the Kingdom of Serbia. This began with an uprising in the year 1804 and with progressive expansion of the territory resulted in the territory of Serbia reaching the boundaries that it shows here. Nevertheless at this time the Ottoman Empire had substantial holdings throughout south-eastern Europe, but was discernibly in economic and administrative decline. Its decline was hastened by a large peasant rebellion, which began in the year 1875 and resulted in Serbia and Montenegro coming to the aid of the Orthodox, Serbian Orthodox peasants in Bosnia. In a war with the Ottoman Empire they were soundly defeated and Russia entered the war on behalf of Serbia and Montenegro, resulting in the final analysis in a large pan-European conference known as the Congress of Berlin. The Congress of Berlin in 1878 redrew the map of the Balkans. As a result of that congress Austria-Hungary, also known as the Habsburg Empire, represented here by the area in blue, was given Bosnia and Herzegovina to occupy and administer. We are ready for the next map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can turn once again, Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher -- I believe this is Exhibit 13. Before we move to Exhibit 13, we would move Exhibit 12, the Balkan peninsula map, 1877, into evidence. I believe with regard to this next exhibit, Mr. Donia, the Balkan peninsula 1878-1912, which has been marked as Exhibit 13, that is the same source as the prior map, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Paul Robert Magocsi, the historical Atlas of East Central Europe. The largest change to note in this map is that Bosnia has now become blue, reflecting the domination of Austria-Hungary in Bosnia. Additionally Serbia has become internationally recognised as independent, as was its small neighbour, Montenegro for some time, and a corridor of land separates the two, Serbia and Montenegro, which is the area known as the Sanjak of Novi Pazar. The Austro-Hungarian period in Bosnia lasted from 1878 to 1918. This period was -- ushered in the era of modernisation in Bosnia and set off substantial changes in its political life. It meant the arrival of a central, highly organised state apparatus and bureaucracy, the development of transportation and communication infrastructure, the development of a periodical press and industrialisation. It also ushered in a period of organised political parties for the first time in Bosnia. Significantly, however, the Habsburg authorities declined to abolish the system of dues that was owed by Christian peasants to Muslim landlords. Instead, they formalised and codified them in law. Thus it was that the tension between Muslim landlords and Christian peasants continued during the Austro-Hungarian period and towards the end of it may have intensified. There were some peasant rebellions after the turn of the century. In my discussion of the Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian periods I have omitted one very important development that I would like to touch on briefly, and that really was the rise of nationalism. In Bosnia itself this process itself can be seen as the progressive development from a religious community into nationality. There are several stages to it. I mentioned that religious conversions in the period of early Ottoman administration seemed to be very fluid, something that individuals seemed to be able to undertake with relative ease. As time went along, however, these decisions became more difficult and transition from one religious community to another became more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The religious communities themselves slowly developed cultural traits, which were unique to them. So there arose a whole set of cultural practices which were unrelated to religion per se but which came increasingly to mark one's identity as a member of a religious community and ethnic group. These pertained to matters including honouring holidays, use of cuisine, attire, especially hats, and oral traditions that were handed down from one generation to another, which came to mark people as distinctly a part of one community or another. Much of this endured into the 20th century, particularly in rural areas. Key in the development of this process were clearly the religious institutions, the Serbian Orthodox church, the Fransciscan missions in Bosnia and Muslim religious figures. As a result of this process over time these ethnic groups evolved into nationalities where more and more of the peasantry and lower classes came to identify themselves with a nation in addition to a religious community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So in practical terms, Mr. Donia, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means that the Serbian Orthodox became Serbs, the Catholics came to identify themselves firmly as Croats and the Muslims came over time to identify themselves as members of the Bosnian Muslim group. This is reflected very clearly in some census numbers in the 20th century, which we will get to in a minute. But I think it is important to recognise that the intellectual movements which supported this process of identification took root outside of Bosnia itself, largely in Serbia and Croatia. This process, which is known as national awakening by the students of it, really was well advanced in both Croatia and Serbia before it had a major echo in Bosnia in the course of the 19th century. I would emphasise that nationalism is in Bosnia very much a mid to late 19th century and 20th century development. Those are the times in which one can see its echo having a major impact with the modernisation and developments that take with Austro-Hungarian administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prior to that time, prior to this rise of nationalism, how did these particular individuals -- how did they consider themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's a very good question, and again the evidence on that is not as extensive as we would like it to be, and any generalisations about it, I think, are dangerous, but the most important parts of identity appear to be local identity, identity with a village or region and religion, either Catholic or Serbian Orthodox. Those seem to be the most powerful components of identity. Certainly cognisance of one's role in a social class was very important. That was something that was reinforced by the various restrictions and limitations on Christians during Ottoman Rule. So I would say local, religious and social orientation were probably the most important sources of identity in so far as we can determine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Donia. Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that we shall now have a break and resume at 11.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you can have your witness come in now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe the usher just went back to get him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President? Mr. President, before we move on with Mr. Donia's testimony in chronological order, if I could refer back to what has been previously marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 11, which is the map listed at the top of the page, Croatian lands in the 19th century. Mr. Donia, I believe that's to your right. Could you tell the Trial Chamber the source of that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's from a Concise Atlas of the Republic of Croatia and of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina published by the Miroslav Kulajia Lexicographical Institute in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we would offer into evidence Prosecutor's Exhibit 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So this is document number 11. Which one? Oh, yes, I see which one it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just to take care of some details concerning these exhibits, the Exhibit 13, which is still on the ELMO, is the Balkan peninsula map 1878-1912. It is on the ELMO now. I believe Mr. Donia has previously identified that source, and we would offer Prosecutor's Exhibit 13 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber agrees. You may proceed, Mr. Prosecutor, with the following question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Donia, if we can go back and return to where we left off, you had some comments you wanted to make concerning the Muslims and some of your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have been speaking of the rise of nationalism as a largely 19th century phenomenon. The position of the Bosnian Muslims in this emerging nationalist picture was unique, for the Bosnian Muslims did not develop a nationalist movement with the same traits as the Serbs and Croats did until very late, until, in fact, the period of socialism in the second Yugoslavia. Rather, they continued to define themselves as a religious community. The nationalist movements can be seen, I think, as going through three phases, although at times these overlap a great deal. The first phase really is the attempt to define a cultural community. That's typically based on language, defining a common language for the group. That was indeed the concern of the early intellectual leaders of the Serbian and Croatian national movements. The second phase concerns defining a political community. It comes to concentrate on control of trying to have one's own state. The third phase becomes a territorial one. The Muslims were not able to engage in this kind of exchange at this time because, of course, they were dispersed throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and failed to see themselves -- let us say at this time did not promote themselves as a nationality equivalent to the Serbs and Croats. However, as we look at political behaviour, it's very clear that they behaved in a manner in which they conceived themselves as a separate group. One can get a notion of this by looking at the first formal political organisations that arose in Austria or in Austrian-occupied Bosnia for the Parliamentary elections of 1910. In 1908 Austria-Hungary formally annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina, which ended the ambiguity that existed at the Congress of Berlin and subsequently ruled it directly. This enabled them to promulgate a constitution which led to the elections to Parliament in 1910.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So prior to 1908 it was not formally part of the Austro-Hungarian empire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was given to them to occupy and administer in 1878, which was a de facto occupation and administration, but de jure did not come into play until the 1908 annexation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first formal political organisations that were created in the first decade of the 20th century were for the Serbs the Serbian National Organisation; for the Croats the Croatian National Union, and a second one really, which was the Croatian Catholic Association, and for the Muslims the Muslim National Organisation. These three parties, each based on an ethnic group or nationality, competed in the elections in 1910 and won the majority of seats, although I would emphasise that this election was on a very limited franchise using a curia system that was used in Austria-Hungary at that time, and thus the number of voters was a small percentage of the total population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. When you say "curious" ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Curia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be curia, C-U-R-I-A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is that system, if you can, just simply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It set up categories of voters. One enrolled in a particular category for a social class or group in which to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In contrast to one man, one vote type of system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right in contrast to more universal and open type of voting. It was a very conservative, class conscious approach to voting. About this time, starting in, let us say, the 1890s and moving forward, it became fashionable for Muslims who were politically active and some intellectuals to declare themselves as Croats or Serbs. It appears that this was a very limited phenomenon, limited to those classes that were politically active and intellectuals. It was a rather fluid form of identity. While some Muslims would declare themselves as a Serb or Croat and stay that way for life, others would feel very free to change associations, depending on circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was that also true of Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was really not a phenomenon that was typical of Serbs and Croats. It did happen on occasion but the phenomenon which I am speaking of, which I call coloration, to adopt a coloration as Serb or Croat as a phenomenon was limited to the Muslims. Much has been made of this coloration phenomenon by later nationalist writers and historians, with some good reason. There's no denying that it took place. The delegates to the constituent assembly in 1920, for example, declared their nationalities and most of them declared themselves as Croats, the Muslims delegates. Others declared themselves as Serbs, as Yugoslavs and I think one as undetermined. The reality, however, is even as these people declared themselves with a national coloration of Serbo-Croat, there are very few instances of them abandoning participation in specifically Muslim political organisations, so that a Muslim political organisation might include many people who had declared themselves as Serbs and Croats by coloration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We are talking about the time-frame of the first decade of the 20th century?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This phenomenon begins really in the 1890s and continues through the period, I would say, of the early socialist years. There grew up a conviction, I think, amongst intellectuals of both Serbian and Croatian nationalist writers and thinkers that this meant that all Muslims would follow the leadership of their politically active class and proclaim themselves Serbs or Croats. Indeed, much of the dialogue that goes on about nationality in Bosnia in the early decades of the 20th century focuses on whether the Muslims are really Croats or really Serbs. There develops this conviction that if you scratch a Muslim, you will find something else underneath, either a Serb or Croat. This became a vitally important point in the 1940s, 1950s, 1960s and even into the period of the 1990s. When we come to census data, we can look at specific declarations which show that this was indeed an extremely limited phenomenon, but it was important for the political elites at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Moving ahead for a moment, why was that important in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was important because it led certain nationalists to look at the population of Bosnia, to combine, let us say, the Serbs and Muslims, and say that all of Bosnia was Muslim -- was Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or conversely to look at the population as Croats and Muslims and conclude that Bosnia was a majority Muslim -- Croatian -- excuse me -- Croat Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is one of the people that makes that conclusion President Franjo Tudjman of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Writing as a historian in the 1980s, he drew exactly that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue on, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The picture in Austria-Hungary was one in which the nationalist movements of the Serbs and Croats were advancing and, in fact, those nationalist movements had moved to what we might think of the level of state -- the second phrase of nationalism, contending that Bosnia-Herzegovina was for the Croats a Croatian land or for the Serbs a Serbian land. The Muslims on this issue, of course, retained their insistence that they were a religious community and looked back still with some friendliness on the days of the Ottoman administration. But, of course, Austro-Hungarian Rule came to an end. That began really with the outbreak of the Balkan wars in 1912, which resulted in a substantial addition --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you moving back to Exhibit 13 on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A substantial addition of Serbian territory to the south, in this area here, and a period of conflict, the first really in the 20th century, which cast into doubt the existing boundaries in an important way. On June 28th, 1914, a very famous date in history, the Archduke Francis Ferdinand, successor to the Emperor of Austria, was assassinated in Sarajevo by a group of eight Bosnian Serb nationalists. This did not immediately lead to World War I, but it set off a period of intense diplomacy that resulted some weeks later in the outbreak of World War I. There was very little fighting on Bosnian territory in World War I, despite the important role of the Sarajevo event in the outbreak of war. There was a great deal of fighting in neighbouring Serbia and the Serbian military experienced great losses in World War I. But in 1918, of course, the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary, and the Germans, the dual powers were defeated ending this period of multi-national empire rule in the South Slavs lands. That is kind of an important boundary point, because it leads thereafter to the two Yugoslavias, the first one the Royal Yugoslavia, and the second one the socialist one of 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, at this point, as you say, 1918 becomes a significant point into moving into the two Yugoslavias. To summarise, where are we at this point in the history of Bosnia and exactly what is going on as we move into the two Yugoslavias?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the nationalist movements have transformed the political landscape. Religion has always been important and continues to be important, but as far as political participation is concerned, nationality has now superseded religion in terms of identifying the way that people chose to affiliate politically. It also continued really in Bosnia. At this point the situation where a Muslim land owning class had substantial dues paid to it by the peasantry made up principally, almost exclusively, of Serbs and Croats. So while there was a substantial free peasantry, this practice continued right to the last day of Austro-Hungarian administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Moving now to the two Yugoslavias, what date were they formulated, the first one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I move to the next map perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure. If I can ask the usher, Mr. President, to show Mr. Donia and counsel, as well as the bench, Exhibit 14. Mr. Donia, turning your attention to Exhibit 14, what is Exhibit 14 and what is the source for that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map that appears in a book. I will give you the translated title in English. It is by Ljubo Boban, a Croatian historian. The book is "Croatian Borders from 1918 to 1993", published in Zagreb in 1993 by a publisher Skolska Knjiga of the Croatian Academy of Arts and Sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning to the map itself and using the map for the purposes of your testimony, what is this map, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map of the two Yugoslavias. The top one is the creation -- I will just translate this. The creation of the Yugoslav State after 1918. I wanted to share it with you in part because it shows the remarkable similarities of the map of Bosnia both in 1918 and in 1945, but in any case it shows the creation of the Yugoslav State which was proclaimed on December 1st, 1918 as a constitutional monarchy under the rulership of the Royal House of Serbia. As can be seen, this configuration generally respected the existing administrative units that made up the Royal Yugoslavia. The Croatian lands familiar from this sort of half moon shape was pretty much the way it had existed under Austro-Hungarian administration. Slovenia, made up of a couple of provinces that had previously been part of the Austrian part of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy; Bosnia in this now familiar triangular shape with the very rough edges along the right-hand side, as it had existed under Austria-Hungary with a few changes, and a large Serbian state with its smaller neighbour, Montenegro, consisting of what had been Serbia, plus some additional territories that represented both gains in the Balkan wars and additions thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For the sake of accuracy, Mr. Donia, when the kingdom was established in 1918, it had not yet received the name the kingdom of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. The title was the kingdoms of the Serbs, Slovenes -- Croats and Slovenes and thus was only to receive the name the kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1929. The Kingdom of Yugoslavia or the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was born of a number of factors, certainly the hopes by Serbian politicians that this would represent an opportunity to expand Serbian influence in the new state; by Croatian politicians with the hope that in an equitable South Slavs political entity could be created, and a desire to prevent additional accusations of their territory by Italy, which was an important factor at that time, and by the idealistic views of Wilsonian politicians and diplomats, who hoped to create states based on nationalist aspirations. It was, however, a State that was beset from early on by severe questions of national organisation. It had a central Parliament and in an event that was to touch off many subsequent developments in 1928 the leader of the Croatian peasant party, Stjepan Radic was assassinated in Parliament. He was shot on 20th June 1928 and died in August of 1928. He was a rather controversial and mercurial figure. His death left the Yugoslav Kingdom or the kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in a great deal of turmoil. King Alexander responded to this on 6th January 1929 by declaring a royal dictatorship. This royal dictatorship was designed to dampen the nationality conflicts in the kingdom and he changed the name to the kingdom of Yugoslavia. He also radically changed the internal administration of the state, which should move us to the next map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we do that, your Honour, Exhibit 14, the map of the two Yugoslavias has been previously identified at source and we just move it into evidence and turn with the court's permission to exhibit 15, which I am handing to the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. I just want clarification. I do not want to interrupt your presentation. Why was the Serb dynasty chosen in 1918?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was clearly the strongest existing, let's say, point of political gravity. The Serbian state had emerged from the Balkan wars and World War I as the clearly leading entity in the confederation or the grouping of South Slavs peoples and certainly the one with the most political experience and political independence. I do not think there was a whole lot of question about which dynasty it would be. There was some discussion about what political form Yugoslavia might take, but this was clearly the most rational one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning your attention to the exhibit that's on the ELMO at this point, which is Exhibit 15, which is a map dated in 1929, Mr. Donia, can you give us the source of that map before you begin discussion on Exhibit 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This likewise comes from the work of Ljubo Boban, "Hrvatske granice od 1918 do 1993 godine", which is the work I cited earlier, published in Zagreb by Skolska Knjiga and the Croatian Academy of Arts and Sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What does that map depict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia disappears and entirely new political units' merge in what has been re-named the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. These entities -- there are nine of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are pointing to the map on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, are named not after nationalities, not after administrative units but after geographical features. There was concentration of one or another nationality in them but they were designed by the monarchy to try to dampen down nationalist passions. Simultaneously or about the same time the monarchy outlawed the communist party, which was then a growing political force, and all parties based on confessional or ethno-national affiliations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did this result in some additional hostilities within the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it actually succeeded in dampening things down for a period of time but if left many questions unresolved. It was particularly a time in the 1930s were external forces were becoming more important to Yugoslavia. One looked at the rise of fascist Italy to the west and to the north the growth of an increasingly aggressive Germany, and the next major development that occurs in the history of the first Yugoslavia was in October of 1934, when King Alexander, who had proclaimed this arrangement, was assassinated by a group of terrorists, led by or participated by in members by the Croatian ultra nationalist Ustace. The word "Ustace" means insurgents or rebels. Obviously his reign came to an end at that point and left the authority in the land in the hands of a regent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this point, at the time of his assassination, the nine banovinas are still in place, are they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They remained in place through his assassination. Again under increasing threats from Nazi Germany and Mussolini's Italy in 1939 the Regent, Prince Paul, authorised the Prime Minister Cvetkovic to pursue an agreement with Vladko Macek, who was the head of the Croatian Peasant Party, and the successor to Stjepan Radic. These negotiations lasted some months and were essentially an effort on the part of the regency to establish a working coalition between the Serbian and Croatian nationalist forces within Yugoslavia. They may be seen in a sense as an agreement of the -- which was final reached in August 1939, an agreement between the two largest actors in Yugoslavia at the expense of the smaller ones. This 1939 agreement, finally signed on 22nd August, is known as the Cvetkovic-Macek agreement -- it has a couple of names, which I want to just take a minute to outline -- the Sporazum, which simply means agreement, or the so-called Banovina Plan. The term "Banovina", and these are all Banovinas here, derives from the word that had been used from the Middle Ages, of course, a Slavic term based on Ban or governor. So the Banovina may be interpreted as a governorship. This agreement altered the map and became known as the Banovina plan. I would like to go to that map at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The Banovina plan alters the map Exhibit 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. It alters it in important ways, although some of the boundaries remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we move to Exhibit 16, we will offer into evidence Prosecutor's Exhibit 15, which is on the ELMO, and we would offer to the usher Prosecutor's Exhibit 16, which is now being handed to the court and counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the Judge please put his microphone on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned the it altered the map. In what way did it alter the map? Did it increase the Serbian part or the Croatian part or the Muslim part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will be glad to answer your question. It increased the size of really the Banovina that had the most Croats in it and created one super-Croatian banovina. So it departed from the rule of banovinas as based purely on geographic features and created one which was explicitly national, Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge Riad, and if we can discuss this with Exhibit 16, with the court's permission, and before we discuss that, can we take a look at that particular exhibit, Mr. Donia, and source that particular exhibit, Exhibit 16, which is on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is likewise from the Ljubo Boban work cited in the previous two maps. I should note that Boban wrote a book some years ago about the Cvetkovic-Macek agreement and so it should be a good authority on the creation of this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turn your attention to Exhibit 16, the banovina and explain it please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This small inset gives an overall picture of how the map was revised. The Croatian banovina now becomes a large, almost encircling, almost completely encircling oval around a territory which is left in another banovina and represents the result of the Croatian Macek pursuit of the territorial aims of the Croats. It was ultimately a village-by-village kind of negotiation but became extremely important in the 1990s, because it seemed to define the historical territorial ambitions of Croatian nationalists. It was cited repeatedly by President Tudjman and others in their notion of what Croatia ought to encompass. To cite one person who got to know President Tudjman well, Lord David Owen, after spending much time with him in negotiations in 1992 and 1993, cites this specific agreement: "Because the 1939 Cvetkovic-Macek agreement had given the Croatian nation control over substantial parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, many Croats, not least Franjo Tudjman, never in their hearts accepted the 1945 boundary between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After the war in 1945 it significantly cut back the Croatian banovina, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This arrangement lasted from 1939 until 1941. That was a two year window of time in which the Croatian Banovina was a functioning part of the Royal Yugoslav government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When this was established or agreed upon in August of 1939 was this tied to the ancient kingdoms or the Medieval kingdoms of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was much more based upon demographic claims and really did not reference those ancient kingdoms, that is the Medieval period, so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You just referenced comments by Lord Owen concerning Franjo Tudjman's interest in the banovina plan. If you take a look at Exhibit 16, is the Lasva River Valley area of Central Bosnia included in this 1939 banovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Lasva Valley of Central Bosnia -- I will attempt to point out about where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are pointing to the map on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is about at this extreme north-west salient or north-west portion of this salient stretching into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That would be in the area of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. South and perhaps slightly east of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we proceed, we would move into evidence Exhibit 16. Mr. Donia, proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Cvetkovic-Macek agreement was reached under some duress by the regency. There was considerable contact at that time between Macek and the Italian government. It was widely known that the Italians were prepared to support Macek vigorously in pursuit of a Croatian entity within Yugoslavia or perhaps even Croatian independence from Yugoslavia, and so the next two years really were a very difficult period of trying to accommodate the varying interests, even though the Croatian needs or demands had largely been met in the Cvetkovic-Macek agreement. The consequence of much political turmoil in Yugoslavia, however, was that Hitler and Germany were not satisfied and on April 6th, 1941 Hitler initiated an invasion of Yugoslavia, starting with a bombing of Belgrade, which killed thousands of people and brought considerable destruction to that city. In the ensuing weeks and months all of Yugoslavia came under either Italian or German occupation, and also was carved up in an entirely new way resulting in new political units, which I can show on the next map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we move to that next map, Mr. Donia, when this agreement was being entered into by the kingdom, were there other Croatian movements that were growing throughout -- in other parts of Europe that the kingdom was trying to quiet down as a result of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We noted that the Croatian Ustace, a right-wing nationalist group, had planned and carried out the assassination of King Alexander in October 1934. Thereafter the Ustace were somewhat contained, but continued to be sponsored and to some degree trained by camps in Italy. The Ustace, this extreme right-wing organisation, came to be an increasing threat to stability domestically in Yugoslavia and to factor in the arrangements that the Italians and Germans were to make for the administration of the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So in somewhat pedestrian terms why would the kingdom enter into this type of an agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the kingdom entered into the agreement to try to achieve something -- a viable political arrangement over the long-term but also to stave off the threat of some sort of rebellion or uprising, possible uprising by the Croatians, but this is not to minimise the fact that the agreement was reached by domestic forces or arrived at by domestic political leaders. However, the rising presence of the Ustace was a factor. It was a destabilising factor at this time in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This particular entity, the Croatian banovina, existed from August of 1993 and essentially ended upon the attack by Nazi Germany on 6th April 1941; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let's not move it forward quite so far. It was 1939, not 1993, but 1939-1941 was when this existed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So something less than two years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe you mentioned you wanted to move to the next map. I request the usher to hand the next map, which I believe is Exhibit 17. If we can turn our attention, before we begin this discussion, Mr. Donia, to Exhibit 17 which is on the ELMO and can you reference that map, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is from the same source I cited earlier, the Ljubo Boban collection of maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is Exhibit 17?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This represents a division of Yugoslavia by the occupying forces in 1941. The relevant portion -- there is much division both north and south of it, but I would say that the relevant portion here is the large yellow block in the middle, which was a large area of territory awarded to the so-called independent state of Croatia. The independent state of Croatia was an administrative entity under the leadership of Ustace representatives, who were essentially installed by the Germans to administer that territory. The large or rather heavy line running through the central part of the country represents the line between German and Italian occupation forces. The Germans occupied the areas to the north of this line, which runs right through the heart of Bosnia, and the Italians, the area to the south of the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So Sarajevo was in the German area, for instance, and Knin is in the Italian area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mostar, for example, was in the Italian area. I can designate Mostar, for example, in the Italian area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sarajevo, right above it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are Sarajevo, above it, in the German area. On a day-by-day basis much of this administration was actually done by ustase appointees, but the military picture came increasingly to pit the occupying forces against resistance movements that arose in this period of time. Before I go into that, however, I think it's important to note that the ustase probably entered this period with a considerable popular support. What popular support they had they tended to lose when they reached an agreement with Italy early in the war and allowed Italy to annex a portion, an important portion, of the Dalmatian coast.
