That was something, of course, which was dear to the heart of Croatian nationalists, because it had been the heart of the old Dalmatian Kingdom, and made the Ustace appear as sort of lackeys of the Italians in particular. It certainly compromised their popularity, although not nearly so much as the things that they were to do in the period after they came to power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For the purposes of the record, Mr. Donia, you were pointing on the map to the light green area on the Dalmatian coast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. The Ustace Rule was brutal. It resulted in the deaths of many thousands of people. It was directed against Jews, against Serbs, against gypsies and against opponents of the Ustace regime of just about every conceivable coloration. The number of victims that came out of this is a very controversial topic. The Croats have -- as a historian Franjo Tudjman has been at the forefront of this movement -- have given some numbers for losses that are lower than those that had previously been used, but there's no doubt that many tens of thousands of people or more perished at the hands of Ustace in camps that were created and in various programmes of expulsion and atrocities within territories controlled by them. It was, in short, the first great outburst of ethnic hostility done by a very organised group, the Ustace, with backing from the Germans, although the Germans at times even tried to rein them in or make their extermination activities more systematic, if you will. It was a time of horrific atrocities. This certainly helped the birth of resistance movements. There were two principal resistance movements, one which was greater Serbian in its orientation and led by Dragan Mohilovic, a former officer in the Royal Yugoslav Army. The second, which was led by the partisans under Josip Broz Tito was organised by the Communist Party of Yugoslavia. Over the course of time from 1941 until 1945 the partition as a movement emerged as the strongest of these and succeeded in liberating substantial portions of territory in Yugoslavia, particularly in Bosnia, after some extremely fierce fighting with the occupying forces. The reasons for the partisan triumph, I think, are three-fold. First of all, the partisans succeeded in winning British and allied support that had initially at the beginning of the war been directed to Mohilovic and the royalist -- and the so-called Cetnik forces. Secondly, the partisans were prepared to ignore the civilian losses that were frequently inflicted on the population by Germans, German troops in particular, in retaliation for their resistance activities. Third, and perhaps most important for our discussion, they insisted firmly on a policy of equality towards all nationalities of Yugoslavia. This policy as annunciated at several meetings during the war and came to be the foundation of a national equality policy in socialist Yugoslavia once the partisans came to power in 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Going back to the actual war period itself, 1941-1945, there has been much discussion, certainly in the 1990s, has there not, to use the period of time of 1941-1945 to support the theory that all the problems in the former Yugoslavia result from ancient tribal hatred. What is your position on that as a historian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The primary instance of it, and I noted that relations between groups in Yugoslavia or in the lands that formerly made up Yugoslavia have two very important violent periods, and one is that beginning in 1941, running until 1945, and the second, the one that begins in 1992 -- 1991. I think it's important to understand the Ustace approach to the Muslim population of Bosnia, because it enters into the question of how nationalities determined their relations in the years after 1990. The Ustace rulers, puppet regime, if you like, of the German-Italian occupiers, were intent on converting or driving out or killing much of the Serbian population. Their attitude towards the Muslims was different, at least in theory, namely they viewed the Muslims as Croats, as Croats of the Muslim faith, and thus reflected that tendency that I have alluded to earlier on the part of some nationalists of both Serb and Croat persuasion to look at the Muslims as a group of their particular nationality but of a different religion. The Ustace regime took an existing building in Zagreb, surrounded it with -- put a minaret around it -- by it and made it into a mosque, and frequently made a point of celebrating the fact that they viewed Muslims as good Croats and, in fact, in some cases as the most pure Croats. The reality was that they also under the German occupiers established a special unit for Muslims and in that unit thousands of Muslims at one time were brought in as part of the German forces, although the methods of the Ustace came to discredit them in so many eyes that this unit was essentially non-functional by 1944. Nevertheless, there was a perception and indeed a reality that at points in time during the Ustace regime there was widespread Muslim collaboration with the Ustace and their rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So going back in history, Mr. Donia, coming from 1945, how many instances are there of South Slavs killing South Slavs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know whether I can count instances but in terms of large scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, large scale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Instances I think going from 1945 on you have very few instances of that. Part of that is due to the nature of the second Yugoslavia, the regime that took hold and the way in which nationality relations were ordered through much of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe you wanted to move to the second Yugoslavia post-1945?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to return to the map that we began with, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Yugoslavia after 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That for the purposes of the record, your Honours, is Exhibit 14.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the aftermath of World War II the partisans led by Tito came to establish a firm control over Yugoslavia and implemented a centralised state, one committed to rapid socialisation of the means of production and to Stalinist political principles. There was to be one party, a communist party of Yugoslavia, and organised opposition after some very nominal original -- initial coalition period was not permitted. In fact, the seizure of power and his treatment of political opponents on Tito's part was particularly brutal. The new state was created along lines that are similar, but there are a couple of important differences to point out, because they would assume great significance in the events of 1991 -- 1990 forward. Number one, Serbia was created as a smaller state than had existed in the previous Yugoslavia, but with two autonomous provinces attached to it, Voivodina and Kosovo, originally known as Kosovo Metoko. Those were largely part of the Serbian Republic but had substantial autonomy and particularly in the latter part of the socialist period had their own representatives at many Federal bodies. One should also note that Croatia receives a substantial smaller piece of land here, having lost this salient further into what became the Vojvodina area. The map looks surprisingly the same. The political system could not have been more different. The centralisation meant that when these particular boundaries were drawn, they were hardly a matter of resolving conflicts between contending political sources. Rather a submission was set up. It was not viewed as consequential because the party and the State were to be so centralised that internal border issues within Yugoslavia would not assume great importance in subsequent years. This calculation, of course, was completely wrong, and in the 1990s they were to assume enormous significance. In 1948 Tito came to a very strong difference of views with Stalin and the Yugoslav communist party was expelled from the Communist Information Bureau. This break with Stalin in 1948 set off a whole new course for Yugoslavia. Initially Yugoslavia had been really only the east European country substantially liberated from Nazi control by a indigenous resistance movement, but this also meant that there was a firm independent spirit in Tito's government and party, and this led to the break with Stalin. After 1948 Tito and the party felt a need to lay out a new course, one which would distinguish them from the tight central control and path that Stalin had set out. This search led to two key answers. Number one was workers' self-management domestically, and the second was participation in the movement known as non-alignment. For our purposes the result of the emphasis on workers' self-management was over time a substantial decentralisation of economic and political authority from the central government. This was not immediate and it took a couple of decades, but ultimately workers' self-management came to mean less power at the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So on a Federal level did the Federal Government become less important?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It became progressively less important and the republics, the six republics and two autonomous regions that made up socialist Yugoslavia became progressively more important. The decentralisation was also accompanied by increasing openness. Yugoslavia had at one point over 1 million guest workers in western Europe, co-operative arrangements with outside firms and was generally starting to become more a part of the western European economy than any of the other countries of east Europe were. Still this was a period of rapid industrialisation and very rapid urbanisation. To take one example, if one recalls that the city of Sarajevo had a population in 1918 -- say 1910 is the last census -- of about 50,000, by 1991 it was over 500,000. Such growth, while it was somewhat exceptional, was taking place in many of Yugoslavia's cities and in Bosnia's cities. Ultimately socialist Yugoslavia had to deal with some of the same nationality questions that had plagued the first Yugoslavia. In 1971 a period of intense political and literary activity by the Croats led to a series of purges that Tito carried out both in Croatia and in other republics of Yugoslavia. In 1974 a new constitution was promulgated, which in a sense finalised the process of decentralisation and in many important respects set the stage for the conflict between republics which was to occur in the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How did it do that? How did the 1974 constitution do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It enshrined the authority of the republics and severely limited the authority of the central government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that the 1974 constitution was yet another step to make the republics more powerful and the Federal Government less powerful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. By the time of the 1974 constitution other institutions became perhaps more important than the Federal Government in providing internal cohesion to Yugoslavia. Those two institutions at that time would have been the Yugoslav National Army and the League of Communists, as the Communist Party came to be called in 1953.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Presumably the then leader of Yugoslavia, Tito, President Tito, agreed with this. Why did he agree to such a decentralisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was really Tito's last major foray into reforming political life in Yugoslavia. He was extremely concerned about a successor. One might think that he would be concerned about having a strong successor or want a strong successor, but, in fact, he did not want anything of the kind. He wanted to be sure that no-one would be able to concentrate power in his or her hands and so he established both an extreme decentralisation and a very complex mechanism to rule after his death. This was known -- I say he established; it was established in the constitution of 1974. It was known as the Federal Presidency. There were other organs and institutions as well, but the Federal Presidency was to be the principal one. The Presidency was to elect a President or have a President which would rotate annually. Each of the constituent entities of Yugoslavia was to have one person in line for that Presidency. So the rotation came to be by republic or entity and for only one year. As it turned out, this effectively paralysed the institution of the Presidency after Tito's death on March 4th -- May 4th, 1980. The death of Tito, in fact, was widely expected to set off some sort of internal turbulence in Yugoslavia. Surprisingly to many people it did not, and it would be another 11 years before actual disintegration physically started taking place. However, developments in the 1980s did move towards the ultimate disintegration of the country in several respects. First of all, discussion and political dialogue became increasingly free. The constraints that had been there during socialism gradually fell away and one saw in the 1980s throughout Yugoslavia the emergence of an aggressive, investigative free press. This converged with the process of decentralisation to by the late 1980s create pressures for pluralism in all republics of Yugoslavia. The economic crisis was another factor that brought this to bear. There was a hyper-inflation that developed starting in the mid-1980s and brought under control only briefly in 1989, but economically Yugoslavia probably deteriorated substantially from the time of Tito's death until 1990. Finally -- additionally, there came to be an increasing nationalist dialogue in Yugoslavia and in 1987 with the rise of the leader Slobodan Milosevic in Serbia, for the first time we saw the Serbian Communist Party essentially taken over by people devoted to a nationalist programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, Mr. Donia in the various republics and specifically Serbia, Bosnia and Croatia are having problems in the 1980s, but those problems are different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are different, and one must keep in mind that the republics are contending with one another for Federal resources during this period, not nationalities per se. So the fact that Bosnia, which was a republic that had three nationalities within it, was contending for resources with, let us say, Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro and Macedonia or whatever, meant that in many cases members of those nationalities in Bosnia were working together to promote The Republic's interest. So the outbreak of pluralism, if you will, or the advent of pluralism in Bosnia, which can be traced perhaps to 1987 takes a different form. It did not take a specifically nationalist form in the years from 1987-1989. The first evidence of a perhaps breach in the wall was in August of 1987, when a scandal became public knowledge surrounding the enterprise called Agrocomerc, which is an enterprise which produced food stuffs in north-western Bosnia. This scandal concerned the issuance of bonds. It reminds one very much of an American junk bond scandal. It set off a series of revelations and accusations about use of public funds and basically bonds that were not backed by collateral. It resulted through this chain of events in the resignation of Hamdija Pozderac, who was then a member of the Federal Presidency from Bosnia, and in this complex process of rotation that I have mentioned was next in line to become President of the Presidency. The manager of Agrocomerc, Fikret Abdic, was arrested, jailed and this long investigation began, which actually never brought any final conclusion. Then in April of 1988 the Neum scandal took place. This was the accusation, and a very true one, that the leaders of the Bosnian party were using public funds and the advantages that came to them as party leaders to build luxury villas on the one small outlet that Bosnia enjoyed on the Adriatic coast. This was really a scandal that was broken by investigative journalists and supported by the Socialist Youth Alliance of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which subsequently opposed some appointments of the old guard to government posts. Thus we see this coalition in Bosnia between youth, particularly members of the Socialist Youth Alliance, and investigative journalists resulting in pluralism being introduced and open discussion being introduced in the organs of the League of Communists of Bosnia. This was a generation conflict more than an ethnic or national one as it took place in Bosnia. In November 1988 there was an investigation of student dissent at Sarajevo University by Bosnian police, which resulted in again exposure in the press and in April of 1989 the Bosnian Republican Assembly adopted constitutional amendments favouring more democratic elections, a market economy and limiting powers of the Bosnian presidency. Now this was really the very familiar east European way of emerging pluralism under the auspices of existing representative bodies or leadership. In a sense the Bosnian Republic Assembly voted itself into an era of democracy. This happened in one form or another in all republics and in many places throughout Eastern Europe. The actual demise of Yugoslavia, and let us say Yugoslav central institutions, can really be traced to January of 1990, when to try to address all the conflicts that were going, constitutional, economic, there was an extraordinary party congress convened of the League of Communists. The 14th extraordinary party congress. In the extensive discussion no agreement was reached and the Slovene delegation shortly followed by the Croatian delegation walked out of the 14th party congress, and the congress subsequently adjourned indefinitely. This removed for all practical purposes the League of Communists of Yugoslavia as a central institution that could provide coherence to Yugoslavia and left only one institution claiming effectively to represent a force for unity, that of the Yugoslav National Army. The constitutional changes had indeed provided for the pluralist elections in each republic in 1990. There was an effort to have an election across all of Yugoslavia, which was never held because of opposition from some groups, but it brought about the election that we began our discussion with, which brought national leaders to power in each republic and in Bosnia in November 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, just prior to this election in Bosnia in November 1990, looking back at the history and the historical era as well as the two Yugoslavias, what do you as a historian see where we are and what conclusions have you drawn on the State of Yugoslavia at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the first observation to make is that the Yugoslavia of 1990 was an extremely different place than it had been at the turn of the 20th century. It was an extremely modernised country, highly urbanised relative to what it had been 90 years before. It had gone through two political efforts to create an entity which would meet the aspirations of various South Slavs groups, and clearly these had not been successful. Nevertheless there was widespread belief and support for the notion that people could get along and could reach a constitutional political arrangement that would keep the place in one manner or another intact. This was really the rise of a confederational approach to political organisation. It was also a society in which nationalist political activity was assuming very important forms. It was coming to the forefront. As was the case in other places in Europe, in Eastern Europe, socialism had been widely discredited as an economic system, and the centralised, single party system had clearly been discredited as a political system as well. This, I think, left Yugoslavia in general and Bosnia in particular in a search for an arrangement with which it could move forward into the 1990s on the basis of either a coalition or constitutional arrangement that would keep the aspirations of all groups together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are going to move into an entirely separate area. I know, Mr. President, you mentioned that generally you would want to end at 1 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. That is why, Mr. Prosecutor, I think that we can conclude the testimony at this stage with the 1990s. So I propose we now rise and meet again at 3.00 pm with the continuation of the testimony by Mr. Donia. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I ask the Registrar to have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, perhaps the usher could have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He stepped out to do that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Since he is not here, Mr. Kehoe, do you think that his deposition is going to take all afternoon? Is it going to continue tomorrow? What do you think it's going to be in terms of time? I know you do not have the answers he is going to give you but at least you have the questions you are going to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do have the questions, your Honour. I believe that we will finish with Mr. Donia this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. So then possibly -- we will talk about it a little bit later -- you can let us know whether there are other witnesses for the rest of the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I hope you have rested a bit, got your strength back and are prepared to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we begin, just for record-keeping purposes, we would like to introduce Exhibit 17, which was the 1941 map that Mr. Donia referenced this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise, with the permission of the usher, we would ask that Prosecutor's Exhibit 5, which is the map of Yugoslavia from 1991, and I believe it is just to the right of Mr. Donia, if we could put that on the ELMO. Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Donia, we left off this morning finishing with 1990, and I ask you, sir, that after the post-1990 period are there certain trends that you recognise that added to and contributed to the catastrophic events that we saw in Central Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We have thus far proceeded somewhat chronologically, and I find that it's easier to understand these events after 1990 by approaching them in terms of the major trends that took place in the area and just to look forward on the outline that I prepared. These are, first of all, the variants of nationalism; secondly, what might be called the greater Serbian coalition, and its role in Bosnia in particular; third, the strengthening of the armies of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina; fourth, the involvement of the international community in the lands that made up Yugoslavia, especially Bosnia; and, finally, the transformation of the Croatian democratic union in Bosnia, these are the five trends that I would like to discuss in the period after 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say this these trends are going on at the same time in many cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are going on simultaneously and sometimes are difficult to disentangle, but we will strike to look at them separately with a hope to understanding the sequence of events as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first of these is the variance of nationalism. I had mentioned that nationalist leaders came to power in the elections of 1990 in all republics and in Bosnia representatives of the three primary nationalities came to dominate the post-1990 assembly. Nevertheless the forms that nationalism took were quite different as it emerged in this post-1990 period. For President Milosevic of Serbia and Serbian nationalism, I think the word that best describes the nature of nationalism is expediency. The nature of Milosevic's nationalism was such that he encouraged many of his followers to take to the streets in demonstrations which had as their objective the intimidation of the existing Communist Party leadership in virtually all republics, including Montenegro, Kosovo, Vojvodina and an attempt to do so in Slovenia. The result of that was that several of the leaderships of those provinces in the course of 1988 resigned and were replaced by people more loyal to Milosevic's notion of a greater Serbia. In March of 1989 the Serbian assembly voted certain constitutional amendments, which basically ended -- functionally ended the autonomy that Kosovo and Vojvodina -- let me point these out here -- Vojvodina the autonomous area to the north of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are pointing to a map on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And Kosovo which had a large Albanian population to the south of Serbia. These areas were subject to having their political and security organs suspended by the Serbian assembly after March of 1989. With this constitutional amendment in place and new powers derived from his control of the assembly or the leaderships of those areas and Montenegro, Milosevic was in a relatively strong position to dominate events within the Yugoslav Federation from that point on. However, it turned out that Milosevic's nationalism was largely a tool of convenience, and he subsequently abandoned that strategy in the course of the mid-1990s. Owing to various pressures that were put upon him largely by the international community and other requirements he adopted a course which has become in the meantime something very different from the nationalism that he was espousing in the late 1980s. Without going into a great deal of detail about the political nature of that, I feel the word to describe the official nationalism as it came out of Milosevic's Serbia is really "expediency". For the Bosnian Muslims I think the word is "flexibility". The Bosnian Muslims have historically in the 20th century been much more comfortable with a multi-ethnic, plural religious society than other movements of ethnic identity and nationalism. Part of that is due to their historical situation in the middle of these two zones of influence, east and west, and living in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is itself a multi-ethnic society. In the 1990 elections the leading vote-getter for the presidency was, in fact, Fikret Abdic, who we met earlier as the manager of the Agrocomerc enterprise who, if anything, had a more secular orientation than President Izetbegovic. Abdic declined to become President of the Bosnian Presidency and returned to his regional enclave in Bihac and Izetbegovic subsequently became President. Once Izetbegovic assumed the Presidency of Bosnia in 1990, he, together with the President of Macedonia, was the primary mover in an effort to find a confederational solution to the disintegration of the Yugoslav federation. This occurred in a series of talks in early 1991 from January through late March, known as the YU talks. These clearly did not result in the kind of outcome that either he or his Macedonian colleague might have liked, in large measure because President Milosevic was able to frustrate many of these aims, but clearly it was the intent of Izetbegovic to seek a confederation solution, which would provide for continued ties but very loose ties of the various components of the Yugoslav Federation. For the Croatians if there is a word to describe the nature of Croatian nationalism in this post-1990 period, I believe it is "consistency". The tone and direction of Croatia's nationalism has been set more than anything else by Croatia's current President, President Tudjman. In writings that go back to his days as a historian, and there are substantial writings from that period, viewpoints from which he appears never to have wavered and, in fact, President Tudjman has never disguised his annexationist intentions towards Bosnia and Herzegovina. In a work that he produced for publication in English in the United States in 1981 entitled "Nationalism in Contemporary Europe" he spelt out some of these views. I believe we have ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the court's permission, can I ask the usher to distribute what has been marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 18? Your Honour, this is the only exhibit we have that has not been translated into French as yet, but it will be. Mr. Donia, before we talk specifically about the pages annexed to Prosecutor's Exhibit 18, tell us a little bit about this book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This book is entitled "Nationalism and Contemporary Europe". It was published at about the same time in the language then known as Serbo-Croatian in Munich, and was subsequently reprinted in Croatian in Zagreb in 1990. The excerpt that we are looking at is the United States Library of Congress copy of this work in English published by East European Monographs of Boulder, Colorado, and distributed by Colombia University Press.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now as we page through Prosecutor's Exhibit 18, the index indicates that there are numerous issues discussed in this volume; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's fair to characterise this as a very learned and wide-ranging work with vision and scope, which has one portion of it devoted to the questions involved with Yugoslav nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The point -- the pages from that volume that we have annexed to the exhibit, can you address yourself to those particular pages? I am referring to pages 112 through 115?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. May I have another copy perhaps of the exhibit? It's a little bit difficult to ... thank you. At the last paragraph on page 112 begins where I'm pointing here. We see that again writing as a historian here Dr Tudjman writes a chart passage regarding the post-World War II decision to unite the Vojvodina as an autonomous area with Serbia or associate it with Serbia. He writes: "Several reasons could be given in favour of the decision to unite Vojvodina with Serbia. The two areas had strong historical, national, economic and cultural ties and their union was also in the interest of the state community as a whole. The fixing of the boundaries for Vojvodina and Serbia is a different question and will be discussed later. However, there are many indications" -- I tell you there are some typographical errors in this passage -- "there are many indications that the same logical criteria were not applied to the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which according to the same yardstick should have been part of the Croatian Federal unit. Bosnia and Herzegovina was declared a separate Federal Republic within the borders established during the Turkish occupation".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Slow down just a bit while you are reading it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "But large parts of Croatia had been incorporated into Bosnia by the Turks. Furthermore, Bosnia and Herzegovina were historically linked with Croatia and they together comprise an indivisible, geographic and economic entity. Bosnia and Herzegovina occupy the central part of this whole, separating southern", that is the coastal Dalmatian area, "from northern Pannonia", that area closest to Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you just flip the map back on the ELMO and point to what we are talking about there. With the assistance of the usher, could you put Exhibit 5 back on the ELMO? If you could use that map, Mr. Donia, to describe what Dr Tudjman is talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me read the sentence again: "Bosnia and Herzegovina occupy the central part of this whole". He is speaking here to this large triangular area: " ... separating southern (Dalmatian) from northern (Pannonian) Croatia. The creation of a separate Bosnia and Herzegovina makes the territorial and geographic position of Croatia extremely unnatural in the economic sense and therefore in the broadest nationalist political sense very unfavourable for life and development and in the narrower administrative sense unsuitable and disadvantageous. These factors largely explain why the 1939 agreement between Belgrade and Zagreb", which we have referred to as the Cvetkovic-Macek agreement, "included the following areas of Bosnia into the Banovina of Croatia".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, would you put the book back on the ELMO so the interpreters can translate it for you and for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour. I just took it off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We're right here in the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that you were reading the text of the second paragraph of page 113, which begins: "These factors largely explain why the 1939 ..." That is the point that I had got to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. "These factors largely explain why the 1939 agreement between Belgrade and Zagreb included the following areas of Bosnia into the Banovina of Croatia: the whole of Herzegovina and Mostar and those Bosnian districts where the Croats have a clear majority (Bugojno, Fojnica, Travnik, Derventa, Gradacac, Brcko)". I would like to pause at this point to examine what he means by that. If one goes to the census of 1991 and looks at those six districts, I would like to read off from the 1991 census the percentage of self-declared Croats in those districts. Bugojno: 34.1 per cent. Fojnica: 40.9 per cent. Travnik: 36.9 per cent. Derventa: 39.0 per cent. Gradacac: 15.0 per cent. Brcko, 25.4 per cent. These numbers from the 1991 census are taken from the same source as this map here, which is, in fact, on the back of the map, these district numbers are printed out. Thus in none of these districts in 1991 is there a Croatian majority. In fact, the only way to get to those numbers, to say that the districts in question, these six districts, have a clear Croat majority, is to include their Muslim populations. Indeed, as he continues his discussion, Dr Tudjman makes exactly that point. I go to this next full paragraph at the bottom of page 113: "There is little doubt that the main reasons for declaring Bosnia and Herzegovina a separate federal state was the mixed composition of its population and the fact that since the last century the greatest controversy between Croatian and Serbian political leaders concerned the ownership of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The decision, therefore, to make Bosnia and Herzegovina a separate federal unit was purportedly taken as an unbiased standpoint. Croatia laid claim to Bosnia and Herzegovina on the basis of a common history and the fact that they constituted a geo-political whole. Serbia's claim was based on "natural right", as the Serbian, Orthodox population constituted a plurality (about 44 per cent) while the Croatian, Catholic population made up about 23 per cent of the population and the Muslims 33 per cent. Though the Orthodox population was in the minority as compared to the ethnically largely identical Catholic and Muslim population, which together comprised a majority of 56 per cent ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Donia. Would you just let the usher flip the page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We're right here, having cited this 56 per cent as a majority made up of the Catholic and Muslim population: " ... (which has now grown to 62 per cent) the Serbian side overly stressed the "right of the sword", since Serbia had entered World War I because of Bosnia and Herzegovina and had been a victor in the conflict. An objective examination of the numerical composition of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina cannot ignore that the majority of the Muslims is in its ethnic character and speech incontrovertibly of Croatian origin. Despite religious and cultural distinctions created by history, the vast majority of the Muslims declared themselves Croats when an opportunity arose. This was done in 1920 by the Muslim representatives in the constituent assembly". As a note here, I have indicated earlier that that was the case, that the delegates to that assembly in the majority declared themselves of Croatian coloration: "It was done by the Muslim intelligentsia and masses during the Banovina Hrvatska", that is the Croatian Banovina, that period from 1939-1941, "and the independent state of Croatia", the period from 1941-1945, "which all Muslims and Catholics of Bosnia-Herzegovina at first accepted as their own state. The historical fact regarding the attitude in World War II of the Muslim population is bolstered by many examples in the war memoirs of Milovan Djilas, a member of the top Communist Party of Yugoslav leadership. The fact that the Muslim population was largely of Croatian persuasion was recognised between the two wars by Svetozar Pribicevic, who was one of the most uncompromising champions of Greater Serbian unitarianism. About the Bosnian Muslims he wrote: 'Their intellectuals are in the vast majority of Croatian orientated; and the masses blindly follow the intellectuals in all political actions. There should be no mistake about this. The hegemonistic system in particular ... has meant that the Bosnian Muslims in their aspirations and their views on the future completely identify themselves with the Croats. Any Serbian statesman who fails to take this fact into account cannot be considered seriously'. On the basis of these facts we arrive at the conclusion that a majority of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina is Croatian". This is the argument that the historian, Dr Tudjman, advances. He cites, of course, one Serbian politician and Milovan Djilas' memoirs. One might wish that he would look at the censuses we have taken place in Bosnia roughly every ten years over the past really century, and I would just like to give you an idea of what those censuses revealed in terms of self-declarations by the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before you begin, Mr. President and your Honours, Mr. Donia is going to be referring to some statistics at this point. A copy of those statistics have been provided to defence counsel. Proceed, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 1948 census asked the question of religion and gave the choice to people in Bosnia of nationality but did not include the Bosnian Muslim nationality as an option, so this was a pure case of Bosnia's Muslims being able to declare themselves either Serb or Croat. The religious identity showed that 890,094 people declared themselves Muslim. Of those 24,914 declared themselves Croat by nationality. This increased the number of Croats in Bosnia by about 8 per cent. Almost 3 times that many declared themselves Serbs, 71,125. This was the first post-war opportunity that Bosnia's Muslims had to declare themselves of Serbian or Croatian nationality. Again in 1953 there was no option to declare themselves as Muslims by nationality, but 891,800 people chose to use the identity of Yugoslavs. In 1961 it became possible to identify themselves as Muslim in the ethnic sense and 842,000 people so declared themselves. These numbers continued to rise. In 1971 it was 1,482,430; in 1981, 1,630,033; and in 1991, just over 1.9 million Bosnians declared themselves as Muslims by nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Given Dr Tudjman's comments, what do these statistics indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslims of Bosnia clearly had multiple opportunities to declare themselves either Croat or Serb by nationality. Very few did so. I think it speaks eloquently to the lack of any deep-seated identity of the Muslim population as either Serbs or Croats. There was also in addition to the evidence that President Tudjman himself wrote in his works the observations of outsiders who had got to know him in the course of negotiations since he assumed the office of the Presidency of Croatia. In 1993 -- excuse me -- the observations of foreigners include those of Lord David Owen, who got to know President Tudjman well in the course of negotiations in 1992 and 1993. His comment in his recent memoirs, entitled "Balkan odyssey" was as follows: "Tudjman's nationalism is worn openly on his sleeve. He has one purpose in life: to control all the territory that he believes historically belongs to Croatia, to that end he will use any means. He will do it with a smile, a quizzical look or a fit of rage, indications of the seething activity that drives him on". Warren Zimmermann, the US Ambassador to Yugoslavia at the time of the 1990 elections in Croatia met with President Tudjman for the first time over breakfast the day after his victory. He later wrote in a book just published this year: "Unlike Milosevic, who was driven by power, Tudjman betrayed an obsession with creating nationalism. His devotion to Croatia was of the most narrow-minded sort. He stated flatly and with no evidence: "Bosnia has historically within a part of Croatia and has always been in Croatia's geo-political sphere. Not only do Croats live in Bosnia but most Muslims in Bosnia consider themselves Croats". Finally, the consistency of the Tudjman's nationalism position has been demonstrated by several occasions which Lord Owen reports in his book, in which Tudjman openly and without any pretence spoke on behalf of the Bosnian Croats. He cites an incident on July 9th, 1993, when he reports that over lunch: "Tudjman seemed grudgingly to accept that if the Croats wanted Novi Travnik, Vitez and Busovaca, then the arithmetic alone dictates that they would have to give Stolac to the Muslims". Again in December of 1993 in the course of further search for a solution to the on-going conflict: "As the search for more territory for the Muslims gathered momentum, the Croatian Government once again, and without any attempt to pretend that they did not set policy for the Bosnian Croats, stated to all the EU Ambassadors in Zagreb that there had to be 17.5 per cent for any predominantly Croatian republic and in no circumstances could Vitez and Busovaca be given up ... Their formal position was set out in a letter to us from President Tudjman on 20th December 1993".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stopping you there, Vitez and Busovaca, are in the Lasva Valley, are they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've been attempting to characterise the variants of nationalism amongst the various parties and would add to my comments thus far on the Croatian nationalism that there was another variant of it in Bosnia led by the person who was elected, who won the most votes in the 1990 election, and that was Mr. Stjepan Kljuic, who was clearly a Croatian nationalist, but strongly favoured a unified Bosnia and Herzegovina and the realisation of Bosnians Croats' ambitions within the unity of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I will have occasion to go into his role a bit more later. Thus these three variants of nationalism played an important role in the events from 1990 onward and they were manifest in ways that were at times extremely different. There was no question that there was an annexationist desire of the Serbian side toward Bosnia manifested over a long period of time, and that there was an effort by the Bosnian Muslim leadership to mitigate and compromise amongst these factors. The Croatian nationalist side as it emerged from Croatia may be seen to be remarkably consistent over a period of time. The second trend that I would point to was the emergence of the so-called greater Serbian alliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we move into that, if we could, with the usher's permission, move Exhibit 5, the map, back on to the ELMO. At this juncture, while the usher is fixing the map, we would move Exhibit 18, which is the excerpt from Dr Tudjman's book, into evidence. Proceed, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This alliance was one at the centre of which lay the Yugoslav national army, the JNA, for the JNA made possible the many horrific events that were initiated by Serb nationalists both in Croatia and Bosnia in the periods 1991-1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, when we talk about the JNA, it is the Yugoslav national army, the Yugoslav people's army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. We are using its Serbian acronym there, the JNA. The members of this alliance were Milosevic's Serbian Republic or what is sometimes called the Rump Yugoslavia, the Yugoslav National Army itself, the Serbs who inhabited the so-called Krijina region of Croatia, and if one recalls the military frontier map that we displayed earlier, that is the areas really in which Serbs were resident, in this arc, particularly this area with the capital city of Knin, K-N-I-N, which I am pointing to right here on the map. As of the 1991 census about 600,000 Serbs lived in Croatia. As indicated, they had been there for some centuries, most of them, from the time of the migrations that brought them there to guard the military frontiers or other migrations that were set off by economic factors. The next member of this coalition was the Bosnian Serbs, who were widely dispersed throughout Bosnia, but in the course of 1991 came into occupation of substantial portions of Bosnia which they then consolidated their military control over in 1992, and, finally and most ominously, the paramilitaries who were used frequently by the Yugoslav national army to do the actual work of ethnic cleansing of Croats and Muslims from Bosnia. There are three critical events in the evolution of this coalition, which I will just briefly touch on. The first was the ten day war in Slovenia. In June 1991 Slovenia and Croatia issued declarations of independence. The Yugoslav army intervened to prevent the Slovenes -- attempted to intervene to prevent the Slovenes from declaring independence and met surprisingly effective resistance, as the Slovenes attempted to establish their control of border posts and some key military objectives. In a very few days the Yugoslav National Army command made the decision not to contest the independence of Slovenia with an additional infusion of forces, and after a brief conflict, a cease-fire resulted and the Yugoslav army withdrew from Slovenia, leaving it to pursue independence. Such was not the fate of Croatia which had both a large Serbian population and greater strategic importance to the JNA. The events of late 1990 and 1991 showed that the Yugoslav National Army was prepared to sponsor an uprising by the Serbs of Croatia and essentially to fight a war in alliance with them against the Croats. This was a very bloody conflict. It cost many thousands of lives. It saw the first incidence of ethnic cleansing which took place in Croatia and resulted in a very great threat, in fact, to the existence of the -- continued existence of the Croatian state at its height. There were two key areas which I should mention here. One is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are referring back to the map on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to the map. One is the city of Vukovar, which was besieged for many weeks and it was ultimately virtually destroyed -- I am pointing to it -- Vukovar right on the border here, a beautiful central European Baroque city, which was virtually destroyed by JNA artillery fire, and ultimately surrendered to the JNA on November 17th, 1991. The second city which because it gained such notoriety, the assaults on the city of Dubrovnik, the Medieval walled city, attained great attention internationally, because they threatened an important cultural monument, although the actual casualties were probably much less significant than they were in many other parts of Croatia. That seemed to draw a great deal of international attention to the fighting in Croatia. This war finally ended in a cease-fire in January of 1992, a cease-fire which was achieved by mediation of former US Secretary of State Cyrus Vance, and which resulted in the deployment of United Nations peace-keeping troops in Croatia in the very early spring of 1992. The third event that was important here was the war in Bosnia itself. The Yugoslav National Army followed a source that was in some respects akin to what it had done in the Croatian war in that it was in coalition and co-operation with the Bosnian Serb leadership, and focused its work on assaulting the cities particularly of Eastern Bosnia and in conquering large portions of territory in the western part of Bosnia. I will just generally give you an idea of those, if I may, by again pointing to the ELMO. The cities of Eastern Bosnia which fell to a combination of the Yugoslav National Army and paramilitaries who were doing much of the actual ethnic cleansing lay largely along this boundary of Bosnia with Serbia and also in the spring and summer of 1992 in large areas of western Bosnia, around the city of Banja Luka and areas extending out from it. The Yugoslav army in principle arrived at the same decision that it did in Croatia, which was that it strategically had a vested interest in making sure that Bosnia-Herzegovina did not as a unitary state secede from the Yugoslav Federation and consequently pursued the very brutal and costly war there. If the coalition of Serbs was, in fact, diabolical in its deeds in Croatia and Bosnia, it turned out to be surprisingly fragile in its long-term composition. This coalition first came unravelled or started to become unravelled in March 1993 when Milosevic made the decision to accept the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and asked his Bosnian Serb allies to do the same. They declined to do so in events which we will get to in a minute. That split between at least a part of the Bosnian Serb leadership and Milosevic continues to this day. It was manifest most recently in the elections of September 1996 in Bosnia and again in an agreement reached only a couple of months ago in March of 1997, and it became slowly evident that Milosevic's control over the different elements of this coalition and his willingness to support them was subject to a number of conditions and factors which eventually left some of them out without his help. Much of the strategy of the Yugoslav National Army focused on supporting the paramilitaries in their taking of cities and towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, when you talk about paramilitaries, have certain names through these paramilitary groups become somewhat popularised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two names most associated with these are Mr. Cecel and Arkan, which is a short name or a pseudonym for Mr. Raznadovic, who had militaries that were supported and so some degree trained in Serbia prior to the violence that broke out in Croatia. The nature of the Yugoslav National Army in Bosnia underwent a change in April of 1992, when Milosevic promulgated a new constitution for the Rump Yugoslavia. This was a constitution designed to recognise that Yugoslavia now existed only of Serbia and Montenegro, the other states having withdrawn or declared their independence, but this declaration ended the last shred of pretence that the Yugoslav National Army in Bosnia was anything other than a foreign force in occupation. The next day Bosnian President Izetbegovic demanded the complete withdrawal of the Yugoslav National Army from Bosnia, but the -- there had been preparation for this in advance on the part of the army, and on May 4th, 1992 the federal Presidency of Yugoslavia ordered the withdrawal of all troops who were citizens of the Yugoslav federal Republic. This was an attempt to argue that it had complied with international pressure to withdraw its army. However, it left virtually all of its arms behind and all of its men who were said to be from Bosnia, and, in fact, the composition of those forces changed very little, but did come under the command of General Radko Mladic, who continues to command them to this day. At that point the nomenclature used to refer to the Yugoslav National Army in Bosnia was changed to the Bosnian Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, in Bosnian Serbo-Croatian are the initials normally used to refer to that army VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The second trend then that I have discussed here was this greater Serb coalition with drastic and negative consequences for both Croatia and Bosnia and the ultimate unravelling of it, which began in March of 1993. The third trend I would like to point out because it is -- I will not elaborate on it, but I would just like to acknowledge it -- is whereas the armies of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina at the beginning of this conflict were nothing more than territorial forces, in the course of 1991, 1992 and 1993 they became stronger, more effective fighting forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, let me interrupt you for one moment. When you say territorial forces, are you referring to the defensive plan that had been inherent in the defensive plan for the former Yugoslavia in the use of territorial forces spread throughout the country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the origin of these forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you just explain that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were created in a period of socialist Yugoslavia as a kind of a reserve force or domestic component of the military force intended to assure that any invader might face very serious -- serious resistance from local forces. These were effectively lightly armed at the time that the conflict broke out so, building an army for Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina was a substantial task and, in fact, both succeeded to some degree in the course of those three years in achieving not parity but greater strength, which enabled them to become more effective on the battlefield. The fourth trend was the involvement of the international community in the lands that made up Yugoslavia particularly Bosnia. It will be remembered that the discussions between the republics ended effectively with the elections of 1990 until the Yugoslav YU talks were initiated in January-March of 1991. The international community first became involved formally in this picture when the Slovenes declared independence in June of 1991 and the European Community despatched a delegation to try to mediate between the Slovenes and the JNA. This mediation was successful and marked the beginning of a protracted involvement by the European union, the then European community, as of, I think, 1994 called the European Union, which is the area within the region. Cyrus Vance as the personal representative of the United Nations’ Secretary-General mediated the conflict in Croatia resulting ultimately in the cease-fire of January 2nd, 1992, and the deployment of UN peace-keepers. There were five important plans that were brought to the contenders in the region by the international community. I am going to just identify them. One can probably determine that there were 25 or 50 or 100, but I would like to categorise them as five primary plans brought together by the international community. The first of these was an agreement mediated by the European union on February 23rd, 1992, which was just before the conflict in Bosnia began. The second was the Vance-Owen Peace Plan of January 1993, which I'll discuss in greater detail in a moment. The third was the combination of proposals known typically as the Owen Stoltenberg proposals from June of 1993 until very early 1994. Fourth, just to complete the picture, was the federation agreement between the Serbs and Croats reached at the -- excuse me -- the Bosnian government and the Croats or the Muslims and the Croats, reached in March of 1994, and, finally, the current arrangement, the Dayton Peace Agreement, signed in November 1995. The first of these, the Lisbon agreement was a meeting held in Lisbon and attended by President Izetbegovic of Bosnia, Mate Boban as a representative of the Bosnian Croats and representatives of the Bosnian Serbs to partition -- let me not use the word "partition" -- to create cantons in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you use the word "cantons", what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the Swiss model, that is areas which had perhaps an ethnic concentration in them. It retained a central government with some authority, but clearly the cantons were a way to establish separate areas to satisfy the aspirations of the competing groups. This agreement was renounced by President Izetbegovic almost as soon as he returned from Lisbon. It resulted in further meetings in the next 30 days, but failed to stem the tide that was then moving towards confrontation. It will be remembered that in -- just to identify a date here -- on 29th February and 1st March 1992 a referendum was held in Bosnia on the question of sovereignty and independence and that referendum was a deadline against which negotiators were then working to try to secure an agreement. That effort failed. The second major international plan was the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. This emerged from discussions and negotiations that began at the London conference of August 1992. The London conference was convened to include numerous countries in a discussion of the future of Bosnia, to address the war which was then raging and in particular was pitting the Bosnian Serbs, who were having considerable success then, against the Bosnian government. The London conference resulted in the appointment of co-chairmen of the Steering Committee of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia, which is what the London conference came to be called. Those co-chairmen were Lord David Owen representing the European Community, and Cyrus Vance as the personal representative of the Secretary-General of the United Nations. Negotiations began immediately after the London conference and proceeded intensively, but not until January 2nd, 1993 was the first formal plenary session held. At that time the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was released to the public, largely because the co-chairmen had at that point not succeeded in bringing all parties on board. The Vance-Owen Peace Plan turned out to be the high watermark of Croatian nationalist fortunes in Bosnia from a territorial standpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can ask the usher, your Honour, to hand out what has been marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 19. Before we proceed in talking about this particular map, Mr. Donia, where did this map come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The map in black and white only appears in David Owen's book "Balkan Odyssey".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who did the rather professional job for colouring in the blue and red areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for your compliment. I did. I coloured this in to show -- the only thing I really wanted to show was the three Croatian dominated provinces which were designed in the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are turning to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll turn to the ELMO here and show that provinces 3, 8 and 10 in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan in its original formulation from January 1993 were to be provinces in which Croatian authority was to be established and forces were to be there until the demilitarisation occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was Bosnian Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Vance-Owen --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just before you move on, by way of explanation, how about the red and white areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The red areas were those designated for the Bosnian Serbs and the white areas for the Bosnian government or at that time frequently also referred to the Bosnian Muslims. The Vance-Owen Peace Plan, in fact, consisted of four elements. One was the map. It proved to be the most controversial and difficult. Second was a set of constitutional provisions. Third was a cease-fire arrangement or cessation of hostilities. Fourth were a set of interim provisions for the transition to a demilitarised Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the first available opportunity on January 4th 1993 Mate Boban signed all four provisions of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan on behalf of Bosnia's Croats. The map and the map only was resisted by President Izetbegovic of Bosnia, and the map and certain constitutional provisions were rejected by Radovan Karadzic on behalf of the Bosnian Serbs. An intense period of diplomacy followed, the primary objective of which was to get the Bosnian government, that is President Izetbegovic, to sign the document, to agree to the document. The talks for the conclusion were moved to New York and, in fact, all the delegations made three different trips to the United Nations in New York in pursuit of an agreement in February and March of 1993. After this protracted period of intense diplomatic pressure, President Izetbegovic signed the Vance-Owen Peace Plan in its entirety on March 25th, 1993. He signed it with considerable reservations, expressed at the time as an annex in a report to the Secretary-General of the United Nations. His reservations concerning the agreement pertained to his desire to make sure that the results of ethnic cleansing and conquest, by which he meant the ethnic cleansing and conquest of the Bosnian Serbs, was not rewarded in the plan. The plan did, in fact, call for withdrawal by the Bosnian Serbs from numerous areas then under their military control, but it nonetheless awarded them, as can be seen, substantial portions of Bosnia in the form of the provinces designated. What was the Bosnian Serb position on Vance-Owen? In addition to rejecting the map and constitutional provisions, on the ground the Bosnian Serbs increased their activities, launched new assaults on villages in Eastern Bosnia, tightened their siege of the city of Srevonica and stepped up their pressure on the city of Sarajevo, which had been under siege since May of 1992. Indeed, it's hard to return to the reports of activities at this time without concluding that the Bosnian Serbs were deliberately taunting the international community in an effort to defy and in a sense step up the pressure for increasing their own gains through this defiance of the international community. On April 2nd, 1993 the Serbian representative assembly meeting at Belica specifically voted to reject the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. This was deeply disappointing to the negotiators and to the various members of the international community who had hoped that this would be accepted by the Bosnian Serbs, perhaps with some modest changes as a basis for concluding the peace. This was dismaying news to the Bosnian Croats. The Vance-Owen Peace Plan constituted the realisation of their basic territorial aims in Bosnia, which was why Boban had signed it so eagerly in January of 1992. Going forward, the future for subsequent peace plans was uncertain. As the Bosnian Serbs continued to make consistent territorial gains in Eastern Bosnia, the available territory for agreement was shrinking. The Americans were pressing Vance and Owen to protect the interests of the Bosnian government, who they were championing at that point, by awarding it enough land to be a viable state. So the Croats at that point had no hope of scoring additional territorial gains. Once the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was essentially dead, about a month later subsequent events would prove that the high watermark of Croatian fortunes was indeed the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. I would like to illustrate that point by looking at a comparison of Vance-Owen with the two plans that came to make up the Owen-Stoltenberg proposals of that summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time -- yes, your Honour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are resuming the hearing. Can we have the accused brought in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I do believe the usher went to get Mr. Donia:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Donia, in your testimony approximately half an hour ago, prior to the break, you were talking about the current head of the VRS army, the Bosnian Serb Army. You identified him as Ratko Mladic during the time-frame 1992-1993; is that correct? Is he still the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I misspoke. He formally stepped down from the command of the Bosnian Serb Army shortly after the conclusion of the Dayton Peace Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just wanted to make that correction and then move back. Now, you were talking about the particular Vance-Owen map that was on the ELMO previously, your Honour, and that is Prosecutor's Exhibit 19, which was sourced as coming from Lord Owen's book, and we would like to introduce that into evidence. We would like to move on. Mr. Donia, just prior to the break you were talking about some additional variations of the plan that took place after the Vance-Owen plan was rejected in April of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was, in fact, rejected several times by three successive Bosnian Serb assemblies. It was rejected three times by those assemblies and ultimately by a referendum in April through May of 1993. Subsequent to this other talks were held, and various plans were put on the table for further discussion, and I was about to suggest that we might look at those plans in comparison to the Vance-Owen plan in terms of the degree of territory awarded to the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could ask the usher to hand out what has been marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 20. Again, Mr. Donia, before we discuss Prosecutor's Exhibit 20, what is the source of these two maps, sir, that are on this page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both maps are from Lord David Owen's book, "Balkan odyssey". The top map is the one that we had just looked at with a somewhat different coloration, and it is the original Vance-Owen Peace Plan of 2nd January 1993. The lower part of the page was the proposal that immediately succeeded the Vance-Owen plan, the Serb proposal for the union of three republics from June of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The coloration on both of those was done by the same graphic designer as the prior exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now the blue in both of those are the two areas that were given to the Bosnian Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct in these two different plans. The two areas, and again I have coloured the three provinces under Vance-Owen, the two separate areas consist of, first of all, an area in the so-called Posavina area, just south of the Sava River and then a large area of western Herzegovina and Central Bosnia. Just looking at the difference between the two plans, first of all, as it pertains to the Posavina, one can see that the size of the territory has been substantially reduced in this text plan, and also that a corridor has been proposed right through the middle of it, cutting it into two portions. As far as the area of Central Bosnia is concerned, which will be recognised as that area roughly speaking that was a part of the old Banovina Plan from 1939, in this plan much of that area is reduced by a salient of the Bosnian government coming into this area, and also there is a reduction here right around the city of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just comparing these two maps, Mr. Donia, in the first Vance-Owen Peace Plan map in Canton 10 in the centre the areas of Busovaca, Vitez and down towards Kiseljak, at least part of it, were given to the Bosnian Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Going back to the Serb proposal on the bottom of the page, there have been some incursions on to that territory, have there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Were you finished discussing this particular map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Again I would emphasise there were a series of proposals and discussions held at this time which I have referred to broadly as the Owen Stoltenberg talks or proposals. So one must look at a couple of these different proposals to see the point that the Vance-Owen plan was indeed the high watermark of Croatian territorial fortunes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that note, your Honour, can we hand out what has been marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 21? If I give this to the usher. I would also like to introduce into evidence Prosecutor's Exhibit 20. Mr. Donia, we have placed Prosecutor's Exhibit 21 on the ELMO. Could you please proceed, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The source of these maps is the same. Both of them came from a book by Lord David Owen, "Balkan Odyssey", again coloration provided by me in the areas which were expected to be Croat-dominated provinces. The Posavina area in this plan is reduced both in size and again by a small, barely perceptible corridor running through the middle of it. Likewise, the area of western Herzegovina and Central Bosnia is shrunk in this map with a rather sharp protrusion up towards Zenica, this salient that moves up into Central Bosnia. The territory as a whole, however, is considerably reduced in this map from the one that was formulated in January of 1993. The reasons for this were that the new search for a peace plan in Bosnia came to centre around a percentages gain. Once Vance-Owen was no longer a viable agreement in the early summer of -- a viable proposal in the early summer of 1993, there emerged a question for a plan which would award at least 30 per cent of the territory to the Bosnian government. Later that percentage turned to 33 per cent, but it became a question of only so much territory in Bosnia to be awarded, and the fact that the Bosnian Serbs continued intermittently through this period to make limited territorial accusations. The subsequent two peace plans, the federation agreement of March 1994 and the Dayton Peace Agreement of November 1995, I think need only be mentioned in this context because their provisions go far beyond the scope of this particular question, but they did, of course, result in an end to the federation agreement in March and effectively the agreement reached in February 1994 put an end, effectively a cease-fire to the conflict between Muslims and Croats in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Going back, if you would, Mr. Donia, to the Vance-Owen plan as it was introduced on 2nd January 1993 and stayed on the negotiating table until the spring of 1993, how would you term that particular peace plan in terms of the expectations and the desires of the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think it was optimal for them. They received substantial territorial awards, which mirrored in some sense the agreement of 1939 in terms of having a major salient into Central Bosnia, and also possession of a significant portion of land in the Posavina. Subsequent developments were never so kind to them as they suffered some military losses and also were increasingly pinched by the lack of available territory to meet partly the America pressure to award the Bosnian government enough land to be a viable state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Going back to that plan, sir, in cantons 3, 8 and 10, which were awarded to the Bosnian Croats, the Lasva Valley is set forth in canton 10, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's definitely in canton 10. It's close to the boundary, but well within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can move on to the next portion of your presentation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last development or trend that I would like to discuss in this period after 1990 before trying to bring it together for you was the transformation of the Croatian Democratic Union, or the HDZ, in Bosnia from a party that represented all Bosnian Croats throughout Bosnia to an organisation focused principally, not exclusively, but principally upon a territorial unit, that of Herceg-Bosna, as an extension of the Republic of Croatia. From 1991 onward the policy of The Republic of Croatia towards Bosnia really proceeded along two tracks, one, diplomatic and the other military. The diplomatic solution required that Bosnia be subject to possible partition or division, whereas a military approach demanded Bosnia as an ally: militarily speaking the Croatian army needed all the support that it could get in fighting its war against the Serbs and would need to have whatever help would be available from the Bosnian government or the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This, in fact, was a rather sore point for the Croats, because the Bosnians for their part were trying desperately to maintain a position in the course of the 1991 war in Croatia which might keep them out of confrontation with the Yugoslav National Army. Interestingly enough, both courses of action, that is a military alliance and a diplomatic division or partial partition, ultimately could be pursued simultaneously and with at least some success. In 1991, March of 1991 -- this is really at the time that the YU talks were going on in an effort to try to find a confederational solution --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By YU you mean Yugoslav Union?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the various republics of the Yugoslav Union. A meeting was held at the -- just outside Belgrade at Karadjordjevo between Tudjman and Milosevic. Subsequent to this meeting the number of journalists reported that they had discussed or reached an agreement upon the partition of Bosnia. This touched off widespread speculation which has continued ever since without any concrete evidence of a map or specific agreement, but a typical comment was that of the Sarajevo daily Oslobodjenje of 14th June 1991 that there were "too many facts showing that the partition of Bosnia was almost a foregone conclusion".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This meeting was between President Milosevic and President Tudjman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was President Izetbegovic there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no suggestion he was present. Again I would emphasise that this is not something that we can state with certainty was concluded or discussed, but it was the subject of widespread speculation thereafter. In May of 1992 an agreement was reached in principle between Mate Boban, speaking for the Bosnian Croats, and Radovan Karadzic, speaking for the Bosnian Serbs, in Graz, which referenced the efforts then on-going of the European Community to seek a resolution to the conflict in Bosnia. Thus discussions or speculation of discussions was rampant at this period of time really about the possibility of partition. It was considered an issue that was very much on the table in terms of both the Serbs and Croats at this time. On the other hand, the elections of 1990 brought to power as the leading vote-getter of the Croatian democratic community Stjepan Kljuic, who was committed to a unified Bosnia, and opposed to plans of partition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the election taking place in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. He was the leader elected -- became the President of the Croatian Democratic Union, the political party, in the wake of the 1990 elections. The transformation of this party from a supporter of a unified and sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina into an advocate for a territorial unit as an extension of the Republic of Croatia occurred in several stages, and I will briefly outline the primary events that occurred in this transformation. The first occurred in November of 1991 in two separate meetings on November 12th and November 18th, in which the Croatian Community of the Bosnian Posavina was established, the Posavina area being this one there, although I would hasten to point out that the time we are talking about is well before the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, and on 18th November the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or Herceg-Bosnia as the political, cultural, economic and territorial union of Bosnia-Herzegovina Croats. At that meeting Mate Boban was elected the head of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This latter meeting was by far the most important one, because it created and identified certain districts in Bosnia that were to be a part of this Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.
