The context in terms of time was that this is the low point, the nadir of Croatian fortunes in Croatia itself. Vukovar surrendered on 17th November 1991, so the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna occurs one day later and at the same time the war in Bosnia is still several months away. This is a time of critical -- it's a critical time for the survival of the Croatian state and at the same time one well in advance of the outbreak of hostilities in Bosnia or even the Bosnian resolution on sovereignty and independence. I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could, your Honour, turn to the next map, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 22, and if I have not done it for the record purposes, as the usher is handing that out, the Prosecutor would like to enter into evidence Exhibits 20 and 21, the two prior maps that Mr. Donia spoke about from Mr. Owen's treatise or book. Turning your attention to Exhibit 22, sir, what is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map that I have created with the assistance of your staff, sir, which simply stakes the provinces that are named in the proclamation of 18th November 1991 and draws a line around them. These were -- they are solicited in the proclamation of 18th November 1991 -- are the districts which are included in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I would like to note two exceptions which make this a little bit more difficult, and that is that Trebinje here, the district immediately adjacent to Montenegro, was, in fact, just overlooked the city of Dubrovnik, and the proclamation for the formation of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna indicated that only part of that district was to become a part of the community. In fact, the distribute of Trebinje is overwhelmingly Serbian in ethnic composition. So I think it stands to reason that that was a military-driven determination. The same is true of the province of Skender Vakuf, not all of which was to be included in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were there any restrictions on the rest of the municipalities or opstinas that are set forth in this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that were all included in the proclamation. Now this proclamation which was announced publicly on 18th November essentially established a state-like apparatus parallel to that of the political party of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and was directed at a diametrically opposed goal. If the party was at this time and the party leadership at this time issuing proclamations denouncing Serbian, Bosnian Serbian activities as contributing to the ghettorisation of Bosnia, the Croatian Community, on the other hand, was engaging in an act at this time that was remarkably similar to what the Serbs were doing at the very same time establishing a separate community on a purely territorial basis. What was the ethnic composition of this very widespread area of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may at this point, your Honour, I would like to hand out Prosecutor's Exhibit 22 -- excuse me -- 23, if I can give it to the usher. You have before you, Mr. Donia, a series of statistics, of population statistics matched to the municipalities set forth in the map for Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What are the source of these statistics, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The statistics were taken from the 1991 census, and that's on the back of the original of this document, among other places, and the break-down by Croats, Muslims and Serbs was determined from those sources and then a percentage was calculated next to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who put it in this format?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I put it in this format. I just simply extracted from the census data the information pertinent to these districts. This answers the question of the composition, the ethnic composition of Herceg-Bosna which was to be a Croatian Community. If you take all the districts combined, it consisted of 46 per cent Croats. If one again includes the Muslims in the number of Croats one could add another 33 per cent and come up with a number of about 79 per cent Croats. In terms of the percentage of Croats within Bosnia who were included in Herceg-Bosna, the 1991 census revealed a total number of Croats of 755,895; in other words, a little over 50 per cent of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were included in the territorial concept of Herceg-Bosna. The rest remained outside of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So what was the approximate percentage of Bosnian Croats that were left outside of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 40 per cent. Now some of those were included in the Posavina so it is probably a little bit lower, but just looking at Herceg-Bosna, about 60 per cent were included. The next exhibit -- I want to just take the two districts of Trebinje and Skender Vakuf out of this picture, because they were included only partially. One can't statistically divide the map that finely according to the proclamation of 18th November 1991, but I would like to at least demonstrate what happens if one takes those two districts out completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We are moving to the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are looking at that now on the ELMO and the answer is that the per cent of Croats just minus those with those two districts out, Trebinje and Skender Vakuf goes to about 48 per cent, 47.99 per cent. Thus the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, established as a territorial unit, did not have a majority Croatian population within it unless one would include the Muslim population of this territory and count them as Muslims of Croatian nationality. Thus the establishment of the community of Herceg-Bosna as a political, cultural, economic and territorial union. The next transformation that occurred was that of the party itself, the Croatian Democratic Union, the HDZ, which occurred in early February 1992 in two meetings, the first on 2nd February and the second on 9th February.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, Mr. Donia. So at the time that the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna is established on 18th November 1991, the HDZ, the elected party for Bosnia-Herzegovina is still in existence and being run by Stjepan Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 2nd February at a meeting in Siroki Brijeg there was a closed door session of the party leadership. At that meeting Stjepan Kljuic resigned. He tendered his resignation at that meeting. On walking out of the meeting he was confronted by the press, who asked him why he had resigned and he said that he would never as long as he lives explain why he had resigned at that meeting. To my knowledge he has not. Press speculation immediately centred on the weakening of the party's commitment to the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, in fact, a representative of the Croatian republic of Croatia the Croatian Democratic Union, the party itself within The Republic of Croatia was present at that meeting as well. One week later, on 9th February, a second meeting was held. At that meeting two resolutions were passed. The first provided for dual citizenship for all Croats who live in the territory of Herceg-Bosna. This meant the dumping of those Croats outside the community as far as this particular resolution was concerned for dual citizenship purposes. Dual citizenship, I would note, for example, would permit them to vote in elections in The Republic of Croatia, something which has happened extremely recently. A second resolution, which pertained to the upcoming referendum for the sovereignty and independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After a very long discussion, four hours, and with three opposing votes, this meeting voted to amend or change the referendum question to include references to national areas, that is cantons, of the Serbs, Croats and Muslims. Now, the resolution was at this point moving rapidly forward. It was scheduled to be held on 29th February and 1st March, and was essentially being held at the requirement of the Bodinter Commission (sic) of the European Union, or then the European Community. So it's not clear what this resolution hoped to achieve in actually changing the language of the resolution, but it put the party on record as adding a territorial dimension to the referendum, one which would award cantons or national areas presumably if implemented to the various nationalities. It represented another step towards the territorisation, if you will, of the HDZ. This was a clash over the issue of cantonisation, which Kljuic had opposed, and Mate Boban supported. This meeting was, in fact, chaired by Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At any point prior to Kljuic's resignation on 2nd February 1992 had he advocated the partition and the carving-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had not advocated the carving-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Like everyone else, he was to some degree caught up in these discussions about cantonisation, and as a representative was clear on his support for a unified Bosnia and Herzegovina, but clearly played a role in those discussions about cantonisation. Nevertheless, the issue was a clear-cut one within the party between Kljuic and Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With Kljuic opposing and Boban in favour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The party, Croatian Democratic Union, subsequently was brought into line with the notion of Herceg-Bosna as a territorial unit, and the footprints of this transformation, the behavioural footprints, if you will, from a party representing all Croats living in Bosnia-Herzegovina to the HDZ as an advocate for Herceg-Bosna as a territorial extension of the Republic of Croatia can be seen in numerous declarations by the party and the government in subsequent months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say, Mr. Donia, as a result of this movement by the HDZ party to becoming a territorial party, the other Bosnian Croats living outside of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna were essentially left out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were left out of this territorial dimension, yes. In fact, Stjepan Kljuic made exactly that point in debating this with Boban in the press, that, in fact, this would exclude a large -- a significant portion, a large portion, not a majority but a large portion of the creation community in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you consider there is a serious change in the direction of the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is. At this point between November of 1991 and February of 1992 we see a 180 degree of direction in that old spirit of nationalism that I mentioned earlier from defining a cultural community to defining a territorial unit on which certain peoples live. The next event that suggested this was in July of 1992, when there was another declaration of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as a self-governing community by its Presidency, and again in November of 1992 -- by this time the war very much raging in Bosnia -- when there was a General Assembly of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and the party, government and military functions were fused at that meeting under the leadership of Mr. Boban. In many respects the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna mirrored the efforts by the Bosnian Serbs to proclaim a separate territory. It proceeded somewhat less vigorously at first, but came to the same conclusion, and the effects of it could be seen in these various resolutions and in the various ways in which the administration developed in the course of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That this was a party, an organisation and a military that was devoted to territorial aims as opposed to the interests of the cultural community of Bosnia's Croats. Finally, I would like to move to the convergence of trends that occurred really in 1993. I have discussed the major developments after 1990 and in many respects several of these come together in the course of 1993 to take us to the events in the Lasva Valley. The first, of course, was the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. It was a remarkably favourable document for the Bosnian Croats, given that at this point in time they had done very little other than the proclamations that established Herceg-Bosna and, of course, been an important part of the military struggle against the Serbs, but in terms of their participation in the negotiations, the discussions with Izetbegovic had come to certain territorial boundaries which were not viewed by many to have great importance, because the military alliance was deemed to be a relatively secure one. It's not possible to understand the developments of March and April 1993 without a sense of how these Serbian outrages in Eastern Bosnia had riveted the attention of the international community and the world press on their activities. To visit the press of the time is to see daily stories about Srevonica, the tightening siege, the ways in which the Bosnian Serbs were attempting to co-opt the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees into participating into the ethnic separation of peoples by transporting people out of Srevonica and out of the city of Tuzla. All of these events riveted the attention of both the world media and the international community on Eastern Bosnia. In fact, what occurred in March and early April of 1993 occurred in relative obscurity from the point of view of the world press and the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, when you say what occurred, are you referring to the Bosnian Croat-Bosnian Muslim clashes in central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and, in fact, from the point of view of the Bosnian Croats, both from the point of view of the international attention being directed to it and the slowly closing door of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, which would subsequently limit their ability to gain -- make any territorial gains, constituted a window of opportunity to implement some of these territorial aspirations that were expressed in the declaration of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Specifically in this time period it will be remembered that on 25th May President Izetbegovic signed the Vance-Owen Peace Plan in its entirety in New York. At this time all subsequent attention was directed on pressuring the Bosnian Serbs to comply and sign the peace agreement. However, Izetbegovic's compliance with the agreement was expressly limited at the time that he signed it. He expected -- he declared to see international pressure to force the Bosnian Serbs to sign and decease -- cease their hostilities against Srevonica in particular. At a news conference on 28th March President Izetbegovic in Zagreb stated that he would give it another ten-fifteen days before he withdrew his signature from the Vance-Owen Peace Plan if the Serbs were not forced to comply by the international community. He denounced the renewed Serbian offensives in Eastern Bosnia, which had already led to the capture of several small towns, villages and tightening of the noose around Srevonica and increasing difficulty for its population. He also reported that he had met with President Tudjman the day before and that they had discussed the growing tensions between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Central Bosnia. He announced that they had agreed upon a central command, a common command for the forces to end those hostilities. At the same time the role of the United States became significant. This was in the early weeks of the Clinton administration. On 10th February US Secretary of State, Warren Christopher, had announced US policy which was a relatively tough one towards the Bosnian Serbs, but by 28th March he had already begun to back pedal in terms of US willingness to use its forces or in any way to support the actual deployment of force to compel Bosnian Serb compliance and, in fact, on 28th March he announced on the CBS programme "Face the nation" that he was basically -- it was basically a statement that he accepted the ancient tribal hatreds historical interpretation of Bosnia's history. He said: "The hatred between all three groups is almost unbelievable and it's centuries old. That really is the problem from hell. The United States does not have the means to make people in that region of the world like each other". This was the policy maker's signal of back pedalling from engaging in the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, what did that indicate to the three factions at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It certainly indicated that the possibly anticipated US active engagement and support of the peace process would very likely not be brought to bear. On 2nd April the Serbian Assembly meeting at Bileca rejected the Vance-Owen Peace Plan for the first time and to many observers the future of Vance-Owen was starting to look rather shaky. On 3rd April 1993 the HVO met and issued an ominous ultimatum. I would like to move to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, at this time I would like to first introduce into evidence the two prior exhibits, which was the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna map, which is Exhibit 22, and the statistics, two page statistics, which are exhibits 23. We next turn to two newspaper articles, one from Vjesnik, dated 4th April 1993, and the other in Slobodna Dalmacija of the same date. Your Honour, these newspaper articles are being presented by the Prosecutor in English as well as French. 24 is the Vjesnik article. Then we can turn to that, which is the Slobodna Dalmacija article. Your Honour, for the purposes of the record the French version of the Slobodna Dalmacija will be Prosecutor Exhibit 24A -- excuse me -- Vjesnik will be 24A and the English version 24B. I also ask the usher if we can hand out the two copies of -- copies of the article in Slobodna Dalmacija, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 25A in French and 25B in English. May I proceed, Mr. President? Before we talk about the ultimatum that is reported in these articles, tell us a little bit about these two newspapers, Vjesnik and Slobodna Dalmacija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vjesnik was at the time and remains the official government publication or strongly reflects the official government viewpoint of the Republic of Croatia. Slobodna Dalmacija is somewhat less -- is considered to be a more independent paper, but both have policies of extensive reporting on matters pertaining to Bosnia, and I would say both covered the affairs of the Bosnian Croats and military matters in Bosnia generally very closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Drawing your attention back to these exhibits and to complete your testimony, you were talking about a particular announcement made by the Bosnian Croats on 3rd April, a day after the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was rejected by the Bosnian Serb assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both of these articles report upon the same event, a meeting and draft six point agreement by the HVO, that is the military arm of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. These -- the draft six point agreement interprets Izetbegovic's signing of the Vance-Owen agreement as effectively transferring sovereignty from the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the interim arrangements that are specified in the Owen-Vance or Vance-Owen Peace Plan. I just go through the six points which are on -- if you are looking at the Vjesnik article, this one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe it's on page 3 of the translation and on the original it's an insert in the right-hand column; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it will be easiest if we just deal with the Vjesnik report. The Slobodna Dalmacija version is virtually identical. It appears that a press release was prepared and both reporters, as may sometimes be the case, made the press release the primary body of their report. So we are on page 3 of the Vjesnik article in a small insert that says "Box". The language begins: "The statement on co-operation ..." This again was an insert in the Vjesnik article: "The statement on co-operation of the Croatian and Muslim people. On the military structure in Bosnia-Herzegovina until complete demilitarisation and on other issues already signed by Mate Boban and to be signed by Alija Izetbegovic reads as follows". Now as background Alija Izetbegovic was not there. In fact, at this point he was on his way to the Middle East, and so it's a one-sided HVO document, and as you go through it, you see there is no prospect that Izetbegovic would sign this: "After the signing of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban are agreed that: 1. All misunderstandings have been avoided between the Croatian and Muslim people concerning the borders of the provinces and temporary authority in them and in the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. 2. All armed forces of the HVO and the police of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, as well as of the HVO army, the Bosnia-Herzegovina army and Bosnia-Herzegovina Ministry of the Interior, known as MUP, which originate outside their provinces shall have to identify themselves and leave such provinces within three days". This pertains to the provinces that were outlined in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So for the purposes of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, the Bosnian Muslim side or the Bosnian government side would have to get out of areas 3, 8 and 10?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within three days. It doesn't specify within three days of what but it goes on to specify a date. Point three becomes more specific: "3. Until the complete demilitarisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina as envisaged under the peace plan", which it did, "and for reasons of more efficient defence against aggression, the domicile armed forces of HVO and the BH army in provinces 1, 5 and 9 shall be placed on the command of the main staff of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army and in provinces 3, 8 and 10 under the command of the main staff of the HVO". Thus this agreement provides for the segregation of military forces into the provinces which were assigned to the respective groups: "Those forces which cannot accept this decision have the possibility to leave the provinces. 4. The main staff of the HVO and the main staff of the BH army shall set up a joint command no later than 15th April 1993". The date 15th April subsequently assumed great significance as a deadline for this ultimatum to be implemented: "5. Conflicts between the HVO and the BH army shall stop at once and are never to be resumed. 6. The free movement of people and goods on all thoroughfares in the free territory of the above-mentioned provinces shall be made possible at once".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So is there a deadline date put into this six point plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The deadline date is 15th April. It is specifically the deadline for the establishment of a joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Alija Izetbegovic ever sign this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We turn to the body of the article itself. Is there anything in the body of this article itself that describes, based on the information from the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, what the HVO plan to do should this not be implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On page 2 of the article in the second full paragraph this threat becomes an ultimatum: "In the event that the statement is not signed by the heads of the Muslim delegation in provinces 3, 8 and 10 ...". Now remember the declaration was for Alija Izetbegovic's signature, but it now shifts to say if it is not signed by authorities in the provinces: " ... the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna has decided to apply the provisions of the peace plan whereby each national armed force shall retreat to their domicile provinces", says the report". This is the report that's on the meeting: "If the joint statement is not implemented, the competent military and other bodies of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna shall implement the said item of the basic document in the territories of Provinces 3, 8 and 10". It will, in other words, unilaterally implement those provisions: "At the same time the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall respect the competence of the authorities in provinces where the other two nations are in the majority". That is the Muslims and Serbs. I would just like to cite one other portion of this, which goes to show that the HVO at this point viewed sovereignty as having passed from the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and that is two paragraphs down: "Since the basic document and the agreement on transitional organisation ..." -- these are documents that are part of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan -- "clearly distinguish between the future central authority and authority in the provinces, the Croatian Defence Council", which is the HVO, "of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall prevent any attempt to establish various bodies appointed by the present unilateral Presidency". This is a reference to the Presidency of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina: "And the Government of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, counties, for instance, and shall respect and implement all decision of the future Presidency of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the transitional central government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in compliance with the obligations undertaken by signing the peace plan". In short, this document, cloaked in the language of implementing the peace agreement and moving towards demilitarisation, permits the HVO to use April 15th as a deadline for unilateral implementation of these provisions. Subsequent press reports to this document report that in various ways the Croatian Community or the HVO is treating these commitments as ones not to be honoured if the agreement was not signed by all parties. There were reports of further blockades going north from Mostar over the course of the next ten days. On 16th April 1993 hostilities again broke out in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Donia, just to back up one second, during this time-frame the hostilities are still on-going in Eastern Bosnia in and around Srevonica, are they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prior to the rejection of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan of April 2nd, 1993, we had a Vance-Owen Peace Plan that was the most favourable territorial plan for the Bosnian Croats, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This announcement made on 3rd April gave a deadline of 15th April 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on your testimony, President Izetbegovic never signed this agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And hostilities broke out in the Lasva Valley in Central Bosnia on 16th April 1993, the day after the deadline; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I have one moment, your Honour? Your Honour, subject to the admission of Prosecutor's Exhibit 24 and 25, which is the article of Vjesnik -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I apologise. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would offer into evidence the two newspaper articles that have been discussed by Mr. Donia, Exhibits 24 and 25, and subject to their admission, the Prosecutor has no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Subject, of course, to the opportunity to read them in their entirety, we have no objection at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Quite. As I said this morning, you will have every possibility to know how much time you will need, and that time will be allotted to you. Therefore, under that reserve, which appears in the transcript, Mr. Prosecutor, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions of Mr. Donia at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I turn now to the Defence and also my colleagues. We certainly have certain questions to put to the witness. Perhaps it would be better to ask them after the Defence has had an opportunity to ask them questions, but let me consult my colleagues first (Pause.). Therefore, my colleagues agree that we will wait for the cross-examination for us to address a certain number of questions for the sake of clarification. What I would like to do in accordance with what we said this morning is to organise ourselves. I should like to remind you that the Defence has not had the opportunity to organise itself to the extent that the spelling mistake on the name of the witness did not allow it to prepare for the witness, that is Professor Donia. That's the first point. The second point is that all the evidence that the Tribunal wishes to have in its record will, of course, be open to the Defence for dispute. I turn now to Mr. Hayman and Mr. Nobilo and also to learn what the programme is for tomorrow. Today is Wednesday. We spoke of Monday, 30th. There's no obligation or any objection to delaying it further. I just wish to remind you be that next week we will be meeting Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday morning, because the whole day of Friday will be devoted to the Tadic case. If you need more time to prepare, we can meet in July. I'm saying that it is absolutely up to you and I think I can speak on behalf of my colleagues. Yes, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I confer with Mr. Nobilo for a moment, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Since learning the identity of this witness, we have learned that he has either published or contributed as an author to two books and at least two articles. We do not physically have those yet. They are being obtained and being sent by courier to us. Hopefully they will arrive tomorrow. If they do, we can be prepared to cross-examine the witness on Monday. So subject to the vagaries of international courier service, we certainly hope to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In that case under the reserve of these objections and except if the Prosecution has an objection -- I'm sure you will not have any objections. Mr. Prosecutor, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I personally have no objections. Mr. Donia is a businessman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am coming to that, Mr. Prosecutor. I turn now to the witness. We are now planning your time, Professor, so if you could come back on Monday, that would be very nice, but it wouldn't be a good idea to make you come on Monday and then the Defence may not be ready because of the mail. What is your programme, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, your Honours, I regretfully have prior business commitments that I have engaged in for next week and it would be exceptionally difficult for me to be with you on Monday or at any point next week. I am glad to be at your disposal at some later point in the month of July for as long as you need me, but would beg the court's indulgence, if possible, for business commitments that I have in the United States next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman? I was going to make a suggestion, and that is because of this error, we are putting the witness in a very difficult situation. Nevertheless, we need to give the Defence time to prepare. Could we then plan the cross-examination of this witness the first day in July, 21st July I think? Of course those are not the ideal conditions, because there will be so much time in between your testimony and the cross-examination. What is your view, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We, with the court, regret the inconvenience to the witness, your Honour, and although the difficulty, of course, is memories fade over weeks and it will be harder for all of us to bring the examination we have just heard into the mind of the witness so that we can examine him on the details, we are pleased to proceed on the 21st. We will proceed as the court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to propose and all the judges have a plenary session on 9th, 10th and 11th July. Also I know there will be hearings within the Tadic case. Then there is the fifteen days for the Celebici trial. So it is rather difficult for me to dispose of the time of my colleagues, but provisionally we can plan that on the first Dave of our hearing -- I think it is 21st July -- is that so -- we will do that. If we can do anything better, we will do so, because I agree with you that memories fade and these are very substantive issues, and this also applies not only to the defence but to the judges as well, and so that is what we will do. The Tribunal wishes to thank you, Professor, for the many hours that you spent with us, to convey a great deal of information to us. This will be discussed by the Defence in the month of July and in the meantime we would like to thank you again. I would like to ask the usher to accompany you out and then we will see how to plan our work for the future. Thank you. (Witness withdraws from court).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the witness is being taken out of the courtroom, escorted out of the courtroom, could I just ask a procedural question concerning the articles that I just admitted into evidence? There are actually three documents for each of those articles, that is the original newspaper article, the English translation and the French translation. I'm not sure how the Registrar wants to capture that with numbers, if it is 25 and then 25A and 25B or 25 A, B and C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would prefer that we add letters, that the first article, whichever you choose, should be called 24, then the French version B, A, it doesn't matter and the same for the other two. What do you think, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exactly. The original will be exhibit and the English and French versions will be numbered A and B, the French version A and the English version B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I salute this specific homage to languages. I turn now to the Prosecutor to ask him whether he has witnesses to appear either tomorrow morning or Friday morning, because, as you know -- or even the whole day tomorrow, or tomorrow afternoon. Do you have other witnesses for this week or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I will have a witness for Friday morning. Regretfully I do not have a witness for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We are at a public hearing. I'm asking you and I say this for the benefit of the Defence too, because they will be having witnesses, and I think I can -- I'm sure, in fact, that I can speak on behalf of my colleagues that it would not be a good idea for the credibility of the institutions nor for our work that we delay and interrupt proceedings in this way and that we do not have witnesses. I recognise the difficulties. Your programme is a difficult one and we on the side of the Tribunal for technical and material reasons were not able to ensure all the days we need. Therefore I'm not reproaching anyone. We are all dependent on technical facilities. I'm asking you, the Prosecution, at this moment, because you are presenting your evidence. Afterwards the same will be asked of the Defence -- to try to make sure that there are no interruptions in the continuity of our proceedings. It is not good for the witnesses, who do not always know when they should appear, and above all it's not good for the debate, for the accused, for the Defence and it's not good for the judges, because debates have a certain drama of their own, a certain sequence, and when that is interrupted, it's not a good thing. Therefore I would insist in collaboration with the Registry we proceed in a harmonious manner. We will hear your witness on Friday morning. I beg you to envisage hearings. You know that the Tadic case will be heard in the afternoon, but the Tribunal intends to work Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday mornings. You have been warned in advance, and I think that you should try to even change your sequence to provide the court with the continuity of its work. We will have the cross-examination they have witness in four weeks, which is not easy, but the Tribunal is here to ensure order, and it will do its best also on its part. To that end we meet again on Friday at 10 o'clock. The meeting is adjourned. (5.50 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: --ooOoo--

procedural_notes.text: (Hearing adjourned until 10 o'clock on Friday morning)
